definition: A function containing yield: calling it returns a generator, and each next() resumes the body until the next yield, pausing in place.

confusables: Everyday usage — most code called 'delegation' is technically forwarding; true delegation rebinds self/this, as in JS prototypes.
alternates: A speakerphone patch-through versus a message relay.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Both are has-a: in composition the whole owns the part's lifetime (part dies with it); in aggregation parts live independently.
anchor: Your heart versus a rented tuxedo: the heart is COMPOSED into you and dies with you; the tux is AGGREGATED — the shop keeps it when you are gone.
example: House owns its Rooms (composition) / Team references Players (aggregation) / # players outlive the team
confusables: Association — plain association is any link at all; aggregation and composition add whole-part meaning and lifetime rules.
alternates: An engine bolted in versus passengers aboard.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Small classes that inject a bundle of methods into others via (multiple) inheritance, adding capability without being a base type.
anchor: Ice-cream MIX-INS: your scoop keeps its vanilla identity, but the counter smashes cookie chunks and sprinkles (methods) into it on the cold slab.
example: class JsonMixin: / def to_json(self): return dumps(vars(self)) / class User(JsonMixin, Base): ...
confusables: Base class — a base defines what the class IS; a mixin only donates what it can DO and is never meant to stand alone.
alternates: A spice rack shaken over any dish.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Composable units of behavior (Scala, Rust, PHP) like mixins, but with explicit rules for resolving name conflicts.
anchor: Character TRAIT cards in a deck-builder: snap 'Flies' and 'Sings' onto your hero card; if two cards grant the same move, the rulebook forces YOU to pick one, out loud.
example: trait Fly { fn fly(&self); } / impl Fly for Duck { ... } // Rust
confusables: Mixin — mixins resolve clashes silently by MRO order; traits surface conflicts and demand explicit resolution.
alternates: Merit badges sewn onto a scout sash.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: A wrapper holds the real object and exposes the same interface, adding behavior around forwarded calls (decorator style).
anchor: A gift-wrapped megaphone: shout into the wrapping-paper cone and it adds glitter to your words before the real megaphone inside blasts them. Same mouthpiece shape outside.
example: class LoggedFile: / def write(self, s): / log(s); self.inner.write(s)
confusables: Subclassing to extend — a wrapper can wrap any implementation at runtime and stack; a subclass is fixed to one parent at compile time.
alternates: A phone case with a built-in extra battery.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Refactoring: turn a dubious subclass into a wrapper that holds the former parent and forwards only what it truly needs.
anchor: A rebellious heir legally un-adopts himself, then HIRES his ex-father as a contractor: same services, now through a signed work order (field plus forwarding), none of the family obligations (inherited API).
example: before: class Stack(list): ... / after: class Stack: / def push(s, x): s._items.append(x)
confusables: Wrapper/decorator — the mechanics are identical; this is the refactoring MOVE that gets you there from inheritance.
alternates: Divorce papers with a service contract stapled on.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Five OO design principles—SRP, OCP, LSP, ISP, DIP—popularized by Robert Martin for maintainable, extensible code.
anchor: A blacksmith stamps five runes — S, O, L, I, D — into one SOLID steel beam; the skyscraper bolted onto it never sways when new floors are added.
example: S: one reason to change ... / D: depend on abstractions / (see codes 461-479)
confusables: GRASP — GRASP assigns responsibilities (Larman); SOLID constrains class and dependency structure (Martin).
alternates: A five-fingered gauntlet gripping a codebase.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: A class should have exactly one responsibility—one reason to change—so unrelated pressures never tug at the same code.
anchor: A Swiss Army knife melted in the dishwasher: corkscrew, saw, and scissors fused into one blob — sharpening the blade now bends the scissors. One tool, one job.
example: bad: Report.calculate + format + email / good: Calculator, Formatter, Mailer
confusables: Separation of concerns — SoC is the system-wide idea; SRP is its per-class rule, measured in reasons to change.
alternates: A one-man band collapsing under his own cymbals.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Martin's SRP test: a module should answer to a single actor; two departments demanding edits to it means it should be two classes.
anchor: One desk phone with two lines ringing at once: ACCOUNTING screams 'change the rounding!' while LEGAL screams 'change the wording!' — the clerk rips the phone in two, one handset per department.
example: PayrollCalc changes for CFO rules; / PayrollReport changes for auditors / # split: different actors
confusables: 'Does one thing' — the test is not task count but WHO requests changes: count distinct actors, not functions.
alternates: Two puppeteers fighting over one marionette.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Anti-pattern: one class that knows or does nearly everything, hoarding state and logic that every other part must go through.
anchor: A 3000-line deity on a cloud named Manager.java: weather, payroll, and toaster settings all require kneeling before it — touch its robe and lightning (merge conflicts) strikes the whole team.
example: class AppManager: # 6k lines / users; orders; ui; cache; email / def do_everything(...)
confusables: Facade — a facade is a thin door over subsystems that keep the logic; a god object contains all the logic itself.
alternates: An octopus tangled in every cable of the server room.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Split a system so each part addresses one concern (UI, logic, storage), letting each evolve and be understood alone.
anchor: A bento box: rice, fish, and pickles in walled compartments — the wasabi never bleeds into the pudding. One flavor per cell.
example: routes.py # HTTP concern / service.py # business rules / repo.py # persistence
confusables: SRP — SoC partitions the whole architecture by topic; SRP applies actor-based pressure to each class.
alternates: A theater's separate lighting, sound, and costume crews.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Software should be open for extension but closed for modification: add behavior via new code, not edits to tested code.
anchor: A pinball machine with a sealed glass top but an OPEN expansion slot on the side: snap in new bumpers without ever unscrewing the glass over the working table.
example: new PaymentMethod subclass ships / new behavior; process() is untouched
confusables: Immutability — immutability freezes runtime data; OCP freezes existing SOURCE while welcoming new modules.
alternates: A sealed console with a cartridge slot.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Deliberate seams—hooks, plugin registries, abstract slots—where new behavior can be added without touching core code.
anchor: A power strip screwed onto the engine block: mechanics plug new gadgets into labeled sockets; nobody ever splices wires into the loom itself.
example: @app.register_plugin('pdf') / class PdfExporter(Exporter): ...
confusables: Fork-and-edit — extension points invite additions from outside; forking modifies the core and forfeits upgrades.
alternates: Guitar pedalboard jacks awaiting new pedals.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Encapsulate interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and inject the choice, so new variants extend without editing callers.
anchor: A chess coach's binder of laminated STRATEGY cards: slide 'Sicilian' out, slide 'King's Gambit' in — the player (context) plays whatever card sits in the sleeve, never rewired.
example: class Shipping(Protocol): / def cost(self, order): ... / order.total(FlatRate()) # or ByWeight()
confusables: Template method — template fixes the skeleton in a base class (inheritance); strategy swaps whole algorithms by composition.
alternates: A DJ swapping vinyl records mid-set.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Smell: one class keeps changing for different reasons on different occasions—evidence it bundles multiple responsibilities.
anchor: One steering wheel wired to two cars welded side by side: Monday you steer the left car's road trip, Tuesday the right's — every turn is a fight. Saw them apart.
example: UserService edited for auth rules, / then email templates, / then avatar resizing
confusables: Shotgun surgery — divergent change: many reasons hit ONE class; shotgun surgery: one reason forces edits across MANY classes.
alternates: One closet stuffed for both beach and ski trips.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Smell: abstractions, hooks, and parameters built for imagined future needs that never arrive, taxing every reader today.
anchor: A house wired with forty light switches labeled FUTURE JACUZZI and MAYBE OBSERVATORY — guests flip them all, nothing happens, but the wiring bill was very real.
example: class AbstractUserFactoryProvider: / ... # exactly one subclass, ever
confusables: YAGNI — YAGNI is the preventive maxim; speculative generality is the smell you find where it was ignored.
alternates: A tuxedo bought for a wedding never scheduled.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Subtypes must be usable anywhere their base type is expected without breaking the program's expectations.
anchor: The understudy steps into the lead role mid-show; if even one audience member notices the swap, the understudy has failed LISKOV's audition.
example: def drain(b: Battery): b.discharge() / # every Battery subtype must drain safely
confusables: Syntactic subtyping — merely compiling is not enough; LSP demands behavioral compatibility with the base contract.
alternates: A generic-brand part fitting the machine exactly.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Classic LSP violation: a Square subclassing Rectangle breaks code that sets width and height independently.
anchor: A stretching machine grabs a 'rectangle' by both handles; the square SCREAMS as both its sides move together, crushing the operator's test gauge.
example: r.width = 4; r.height = 5 / assert r.area() == 20 # Square gives 25!
confusables: Math intuition — mathematically a square IS a rectangle; behaviorally, with mutable setters, it violates the contract.
alternates: A square peg sold in the rectangle aisle.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Valid subtypes never strengthen preconditions, never weaken postconditions, and preserve base invariants: require less, promise more.
anchor: The diner's new heir may ACCEPT more coupons than dad did (weaker precondition) and pile portions HIGHER (stronger postcondition) — but never the reverse, or the regulars riot.
example: base: needs x >= 0, returns non-null / sub: may accept any x, / must still return non-null
confusables: Covariance rules — variance governs the TYPES of params and returns; these rules govern the logical CONTRACT strength.
alternates: Franchise terms a new branch may loosen but never tighten.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Safe override typing: return types may narrow in the subclass (covariant); parameter types may widen (contravariant).
anchor: A vending machine upgrade may dispense a FANCIER snack than promised (narrower return, CO-variant) and accept MORE kinds of coins (wider input, CONTRA-variant) — never stingier or pickier.
example: base: def get(self) -> Animal / sub: def get(self) -> Cat # covariant ok / sub may accept wider params too
confusables: Generic variance — the same words applied to type parameters of containers (List[Cat] vs List[Animal]), not method overrides.
alternates: A funnel: wide mouth for input, narrow spout for output.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Smell: a subclass inherits methods it does not want and stubs or breaks them—a sign the is-a relationship is wrong.
anchor: The heir shoves grandma's BEQUEATHED piano off the moving truck: he signed as heir but refuses the goods. Penguin extends Bird, then throws on fly().
example: class Penguin(Bird): / def fly(self): / raise NotImplementedError
confusables: Abstract stub — abstract methods are contracts awaiting code; refused bequest actively rejects promises already inherited.
alternates: Returning inherited mail marked 'not at this address'.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use: split fat interfaces into small, client-specific ones.
anchor: A 40-page diner menu forced on the espresso cart: the barista must stock snails just to sell coffee. Chop the menu into laminated cards, one per stall.
example: bad: Machine: print+scan+fax / good: Printer, Scanner protocols; / OldPrinter implements Printer only
confusables: SRP — SRP splits by the reasons a CLASS changes; ISP splits by what each CLIENT actually calls.
alternates: Cable-TV bundle versus a-la-carte channels.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: A fat (header) interface mirrors one class's every method; a role interface captures just the one collaboration a client needs.
anchor: A costume trunk versus a name badge: the fat interface makes every visitor drag the whole costume trunk on stage; the role interface hands them one badge saying CAN_PAY — all the scene needs.
example: fat: IEmployee (32 methods) / role: Payable{pay()}, Promotable{...}
confusables: ISP — ISP is the principle; fat versus role interface is the vocabulary naming the disease and its cure.
alternates: A Swiss Army knife handle versus a single key.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: High-level policy and low-level details both depend on abstractions; abstractions never depend on details.
anchor: The penthouse no longer runs cables down into the boiler room; both floors bolt onto a steel INTERFACE beam mid-building, and the boiler crew hangs THEIR pipes up to the beam. The dependency's gravity is inverted.
example: class Store(Protocol): def save(...): ... / class App: uses Store # points up / class SqlStore(Store): ... # points up
confusables: Dependency injection — injection is a delivery technique; inversion is about which direction source dependencies point.
alternates: A wall socket owned by the house, not by the appliance maker.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Technique: an object's dependencies are supplied from outside (constructor, setter, parameter) rather than created inside it.
anchor: A hospital IV bag drips collaborators straight into the patient's arm — the patient never brews its own medicine. Swap the bag, change the behavior, same patient.
example: svc = ReportService(db=PostgresDb()) / test = ReportService(db=FakeDb())
confusables: Service locator — a locator has the object FETCH deps from a registry; injection PUSHES them in, keeping the object passive.
alternates: A chef handed his knife roll at the kitchen door.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: The framework calls your code instead of your code calling the framework: don't call us, we'll call you (Hollywood Principle).
anchor: The HOLLYWOOD casting desk: you leave your headshot (callback) and the studio phones YOU when the scene is ready. Actors who keep calling the studio get blacklisted.
example: app.on('request', handle) / # the framework invokes handle, not you
confusables: DIP — DIP inverts which module owns the abstraction; IoC inverts who holds the flow of control (who calls whom).
alternates: A fire alarm that rings you first.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: The arc from allocation and construction through use to destruction or collection; the object must stay valid at every stage.
anchor: A mayfly wearing a wristwatch: born at dawn (constructor), works the day (methods), dissolves at dusk (destructor) — the town clock (runtime) schedules every phase.
example: obj = Widget() # birth / obj.use() # life / del obj / GC # death
confusables: Variable scope — scope ends a NAME; the object may outlive it via other references and die later via GC.
alternates: A hotel guest: check-in, stay, check-out.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Base-class constructors run before derived ones, and fields initialize in declaration order; destruction runs in reverse.
anchor: Building a wedding cake: the bottom tier (base) must set before the top tier (derived) goes on; at the party the top tier is eaten first (reverse destruction).
example: class B(A): / def __init__(self): / super().__init__() # A's parts first
confusables: Virtual call in constructor — reading a not-yet-built field is that pitfall; base-before-derived is the rule beneath it.
alternates: Scaffolding raised bottom-up, struck top-down.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Code run at object destruction; deterministic destructors (C++) free resources reliably, GC finalizers may run late or never.
anchor: Two funerals: the C++ undertaker arrives the second you flatline, paperwork exact; the GC FINALizer is a distracted cousin who might hold a service someday — or skip it entirely.
example: def __del__(self): ... # may never run / # prefer 'with' / context managers
confusables: Context manager __exit__ — __exit__ runs deterministically at block end; __del__ waits on the collector's whim.
alternates: Hotel checkout versus an abandoned room found by housekeeping.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Resource Acquisition Is Initialization: tie a resource to an object's scope—constructor acquires, destructor releases, even on exceptions.
anchor: A scuba tank strapped on AS you jump in (constructor) that unclips itself the instant you surface (scope exit) — even if you are dragged out unconscious (exception), the strap still releases.
example: with open('f') as fh: / data = fh.read() / # closed on every exit path
confusables: finally blocks — finally is manual pairing at each call site; RAII bakes release into the type so no caller can forget.
alternates: A dead-man's switch on a train throttle.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Identity asks: are these the SAME object in memory (is)? Equality asks: do two objects hold equivalent values (==)?
anchor: Identical twins hand you two passports: same face and name on the page (equal values), but the fingerprint scanner (memory address) proves two people.
example: a = [1,2]; b = [1,2] / a == b # True (equal values) / a is b # False (distinct objects)
confusables: Java's == — on objects Java's == tests identity; .equals() tests value equality, roughly inverse of Python's habit.
alternates: Two ten-dollar bills: same worth, different serial numbers.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: If two objects are equal they MUST have equal hash codes; violating this silently breaks hash sets and dict lookups.
anchor: A coat check: the clerk files coats by ticket number (hash), then confirms by face (equals). Twins holding different ticket numbers means one coat is lost in the wrong rack forever.
example: class P: / def __eq__(s, o): return s.id == o.id / def __hash__(s): return hash(s.id)
confusables: The reverse direction — equal hashes do NOT require equal objects (collisions are fine); only equals-implies-same-hash is mandatory.
alternates: A card catalog drawer plus the book's spine label.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Value objects are defined only by their attributes (interchangeable, ideally immutable); entities keep a persistent identity over time.
anchor: A ten-euro note versus your dog: swap the note for another tenner and nobody cares (value); swap your dog for an identical-looking one and you very much care (entity).
example: Money(10,'EUR') == Money(10,'EUR') / User(id=7) tracked across renames
confusables: DTO — a DTO just ferries data across boundaries; a value object is a domain concept with equality semantics.
alternates: Chess pieces versus the chess players.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: An object is constructed inert and only becomes usable after a separate init/start call - flexible, but it opens the half-initialized-object window constructors exist to prevent.
anchor: Flat-pack furniture delivered in a box stamped NOT A CHAIR YET: until you perform the second assembly ritual, sitting drops you to the floor.
example: srv = Server() / srv.configure(cfg) / srv.start()  # safe to use only after both calls
confusables: vs constructor/RAII initialization (483): single-phase yields an invariant-complete object at birth; two-phase leaves a gap where methods are unsafe
alternates: a golem waiting for the scroll in its mouth
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: A constructor that takes an existing instance and builds an independent duplicate - the class itself decides how deep the copy goes.
anchor: A master forger who only copies paintings from his OWN studio: he knows which layers are paint and which are glued-on photos, so his duplicates never share canvas with the original.
example: C++: Point(const Point& p) : x(p.x), y(p.y) {} / Python: Point.from_other(p)
confusables: vs clone() methods: same goal, but the constructor states copy depth in the type and avoids Java clone's fragile contract; shallow-vs-deep choice itself lives at 345
alternates: a mirror that hands you a solid twin
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: C++ pitfall: assigning a derived object BY VALUE into a base variable copies only the base part, slicing off subclass data and behavior.
anchor: A giraffe shipped in a horse-sized crate: the packers SLICE off the neck to make it fit — what arrives is legally a horse. Ship by trailer hitch (pointer or reference) instead.
example: Dog d; Animal a = d; // C++ by value / a.speak(); // Animal's version: tail sliced off
confusables: Upcasting via pointer — a Base* or Base& still dispatches to Dog; only by-VALUE copies slice.
alternates: A passport photo cropped so the hat is gone.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Restructuring code to improve its design WITHOUT changing observable behavior, in small steps guarded by tests.
anchor: Renovating a plane mid-flight without waking the passengers: rip out and rebuild the galley, yet every drink still arrives on time. Behavior identical, structure new.
example: tests green -> rename, extract, / inline -> tests still green
confusables: Rewrite — a rewrite replaces behavior wholesale with fresh risk; refactoring preserves behavior step by tiny step.
alternates: Swapping the ship's planks one at a time (Theseus).
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: A surface symptom in code (odd size, naming, duplication) hinting at a deeper design problem worth investigating—not itself a bug.
anchor: Something reeks under the floorboards of a room where nothing looks wrong: your NOSE (heuristic), not the smoke alarm (compiler), says lift the boards.
example: 800-line class, 9 params, twin blocks / # compiles fine, still stinks
confusables: Bug — a bug produces wrong behavior now; a smell predicts pain later while behavior stays correct.
alternates: Milk that passes the date stamp but fails the sniff.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Don't Repeat Yourself: every piece of knowledge gets a single authoritative representation; duplication forks the truth.
anchor: Two office whiteboards both list the tax rate; an intern updates only one. April arrives soaked in lawsuits — the boards disagreed. Keep ONE board. Keep it DRY.
example: TAX = 0.21 # single source / total = net * (1 + TAX)
confusables: Deduplicating lookalike code — DRY is one source of KNOWLEDGE; merging coincidentally similar code couples unrelated things.
alternates: One master key versus drifting copies.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: KISS: prefer the simplest design that works. YAGNI: don't build features until actually needed—most 'later' never comes.
anchor: One camper packs a KISS-simple folding pocketknife; his buddy hauls a 40-kilo might-need-it trunk (YAGNI violation) up the trail, uses none of it, and wheezes at the summit.
example: need CSV export today? / write csv_export() / not ExportFrameworkFactory
confusables: Underengineering — KISS/YAGNI trim speculation, never required correctness: simplest thing that WORKS, not almost works.
alternates: A bicycle versus gold-plated unused gears.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Aim for low coupling (few, thin dependencies between modules) and high cohesion (each module's parts belong tightly together).
anchor: Mountain camp: inside each tent the gear is packed tight and orderly (cohesion); between tents runs just one thin rope (coupling). Cross-lace fifty ropes and one slip drags every tent off the cliff.
example: cohesive: Wallet{balance, add, spend} / coupled: Wallet reads UI.textbox
confusables: Encapsulation — encapsulation is a mechanism inside one class; coupling and cohesion measure between and within modules.
alternates: LEGO bricks: strong studs within, single studs between.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Smell: a function long enough to need scrolling, with comments as section headers—each labeled chunk wants extracting.
anchor: A single run-on sentence tattooed down someone's whole arm, wrist to shoulder; readers keep rotating the arm and losing their place. Paragraphs exist for a reason.
example: def process(): # 300 lines / # -- validate -- / # -- price -- # comments = seams
confusables: Large class — a large class hoards many responsibilities at type level; a long method crams many steps into one function.
alternates: A 40-verse karaoke song nobody finishes.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Smell: a method that mostly reads and manipulates ANOTHER object's data—move the method to where the data lives.
anchor: A neighbor who cooks every meal in YOUR kitchen: opens your fridge, uses your knives, then carries dinner back home. Move him in (move the method) or change the locks.
example: def total(order): / return order.qty * order.price / # lives outside Order: move it in
confusables: Law of Demeter violation — Demeter counts dots in a call chain; feature envy asks which class should OWN the logic.
alternates: A cuckoo laying its eggs in another bird's nest.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Smell: raw ints/strings and bare literals stand in for domain concepts; wrap them in named constants and small types.
anchor: A wizard mutters '86400' and '0.21' over the cauldron — apprentices copy the MAGIC NUMBERS wrong and the potion explodes. Label the vials: SECONDS_PER_DAY, TAX_RATE.
example: bad: if status == 3: retry(86400) / good: if status == Status.FAILED: / retry(SECONDS_PER_DAY)
confusables: Value object — the value object (Money, Email) is the CURE that replaces obsessive primitives with real types.
alternates: Unlabeled spice jars in a factory kitchen.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Refactoring: pull a coherent code fragment into a new well-named method and call it, turning comments into names.
anchor: A dentist EXTRACTS one tangled tooth from the jaw (long method) and mounts it on its own little stand with a nameplate — the jaw finally closes, and the tooth can be inspected alone.
example: # -- validate input -- becomes: / validate_input(order) / # the name replaces the comment
confusables: Inline method — inline is the exact inverse: dissolve a needless method back into its caller.
alternates: Pulling one thread onto its own labeled spool.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Always leave the code a little cleaner than you found it: tiny opportunistic cleanups on every visit compound into health.
anchor: A scout troop crossing a campsite: each kid pockets ONE piece of litter on the way through; by season's end the forest floor gleams, though no cleanup day was ever held.
example: while fixing a bug: / rename tmp2 -> retry_count, / delete the dead branch
confusables: Big-bang refactor — the scout rule is continuous micro-cleanup in passing; a dedicated rewrite is a separate scheduled effort.
alternates: Wiping the gym bench after your set.
mnemonic: the FOUR pillars: encapsulation, abstraction, inheritance, polymorphism

definition: Concurrency structures a program to handle many tasks at once; parallelism actually executes tasks simultaneously on multiple cores.
anchor: One barista juggling five orders by switching between them, versus five baristas each pulling an espresso shot at the same instant.
example: 1 core, 4 threads: concurrent, not parallel / 4 cores, 4 threads: parallel
confusables: Parallelism alone — parallelism requires simultaneous execution; concurrency only requires interleaved progress.
alternates: A juggler (concurrency) vs an octopus with eight hands (parallelism).
mnemonic: FIVE dining philosophers around the table

definition: An OS-level running program with its own private address space, file handles, and at least one thread.
anchor: A sealed apartment: its own walls, fridge, and mailbox — neighbors cannot reach in without formally knocking (IPC).
example: p = multiprocessing.Process(target=work) / p.start(); p.join()
confusables: Thread — threads share their process's memory; processes are isolated from each other.
alternates: A country with borders and its own currency.
mnemonic: FIVE dining philosophers around the table

definition: A schedulable execution stream inside a process; threads share the heap but each has its own stack and program counter.
anchor: Roommates in one apartment: shared kitchen (heap), but each keeps a private diary (stack) and their own finger on their own page (PC).
example: t = threading.Thread(target=work) / t.start(); t.join()
confusables: Process — a process owns its memory; a thread borrows its enclosing process's memory.
alternates: Multiple sewing threads through one piece of fabric.
mnemonic: FIVE dining philosophers around the table

definition: Swapping the CPU between threads costs saving/restoring registers plus lost cache and TLB warmth — microseconds each, ruinous in bulk.
anchor: A chef yanked mid-recipe to another kitchen: pack every pan (registers), and the new oven is stone cold (cache).
example: 10k threads ping-ponging: throughput collapses / vmstat 'cs' column counts switches/sec
confusables: Function call — a call stays within one thread; a context switch swaps the entire execution state.

definition: GoF pattern family for composing classes and objects into larger flexible structures — mostly by wrapping or nesting existing pieces.
anchor: Scaffolding around a cathedral: nothing new is born on site — pipes, wraps, and bridges just join existing stones into a grander shape.
example: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy
confusables: Creational patterns — structural arrange objects that already exist; creational decide how objects come into being.
alternates: Tetris pieces locking — rejected, implies destruction of rows.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Wraps an object to convert its incompatible interface into the one clients expect, without changing either side.
anchor: An EU wall plug jammed into a US socket via a chunky travel adapter cube — same electricity flowing, prongs reshaped. The cube speaks both pin languages.
example: java.io.InputStreamReader adapts InputStream (bytes) to Reader (chars)
confusables: Decorator — adapter CHANGES the interface; decorator keeps the same interface and adds behavior.
alternates: UN interpreter booth — reserved for Interpreter pattern instead.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Wraps an object behind the SAME interface to add responsibilities dynamically; wrappers stack in layers.
anchor: A Christmas tree gaining lights, then tinsel, then baubles — at every layer it still answers to 'tree', just fancier each time you wrap it.
example: new BufferedInputStream(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)))
confusables: Proxy — decorator adds features and the client stacks it knowingly; proxy controls ACCESS and usually hides that it wraps. | cf. 328 Decorator (déjà pris): 328 is the language feature wrapping a FUNCTION; 612 the GoF pattern wrapping an OBJECT behind its own interface
alternates: Onion layers — rejected, onions belong to onion architecture.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Puts one simple front-door interface over a tangled subsystem so common tasks take one call instead of many.
anchor: A hotel concierge desk: one calm smiling face; behind the wall, kitchens, laundries, and boilers roar. You just say 'dinner at eight'.
example: requests.get(url) hides sockets, TLS, redirects, pooling — Python requests library
confusables: Adapter — facade SIMPLIFIES a whole subsystem; adapter CONVERTS one interface into another expected one.
alternates: Movie-set false storefront — rejected, implies fakery rather than simplification.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A stand-in exposing the same interface as the real object while controlling access — lazy loading, caching, auth, or remoting.
anchor: A celebrity's body double signs autographs at the studio gate; only vetted fans are ever walked back to the real star's trailer.
example: Hibernate lazy-loading entity proxies; RPC client stubs; nginx reverse proxy
confusables: Decorator — proxy manages the real object's access and lifecycle on its own; decorator just layers on behavior the client composes.
alternates: Secretary screening calls — rejected, body double nails the 'same interface' clause.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Arranges objects into part-whole trees where leaves and containers share one interface, so clients treat both uniformly.
anchor: Russian nesting dolls that all answer paint(): tap the outermost doll and every doll nested inside paints itself too, down to the tiniest.
example: Panel.draw() calls draw() on children — buttons and nested panels alike
confusables: Decorator — decorator wraps exactly ONE child to extend it; composite holds MANY children to aggregate them.
alternates: Corporate org chart — rejected, abstract and visually flat.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Splits an abstraction from its implementation into two independent hierarchies joined by composition, so both vary freely.
anchor: A drawbridge between two castle towers — the Shapes tower and the Renderers tower — each growing new floors independently while the bridge carries calls across.
example: Shape(renderer): Circle/Square x OpenGL/SVG = 2+2 classes, not 4 combined ones
confusables: Adapter — adapter retrofits already-incompatible code; bridge is designed up front to prevent a class-combination explosion.
alternates: Electrical extension cord — rejected, no image of two growing hierarchies.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Shares immutable intrinsic state among many objects, keeping variable extrinsic state outside, so huge object counts stay cheap.
anchor: A forest of a million trees pinned to ONE cardboard oak cut-out: each pin holds only an (x,y) tag; the heavy artwork exists exactly once.
example: Java String interning pool; one glyph object per character shared across a document
confusables: Object pool — flyweights are immutable and shared simultaneously; pooled objects are mutable and borrowed exclusively.
alternates: Stadium wave with one shirt — rejected as incoherent.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Four wrappers, four intents: adapter converts the interface, decorator adds behavior, proxy controls access, facade simplifies many.
anchor: Four gift-wrappers at one mall kiosk: one reshapes the box, one adds ribbons, one guards it behind glass, one hides a messy pile under a single bow.
example: All look like wrap(obj) in code — ask WHY it wraps to name the pattern
confusables: All four are structurally identical wrapping — the discriminator is intent, never the code shape.
alternates: Four burrito fillings — rejected, fillings do not wrap.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: An adapter can inherit the adaptee (class adapter, needs multiple inheritance) or hold it by composition (object adapter, the usual way).
anchor: Two translators: one was RAISED bilingual, both bloodlines inherited; the other carries a phrasebook in her handbag — composition she can swap.
example: class A extends Legacy implements Target vs class A implements Target { Legacy l; }
confusables: Both are still Adapter — the split is inheritance vs composition of the adaptee, not a different pattern.
alternates: Cyborg vs person with a gadget — rejected, translators fit adapters better.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: GoF pattern family assigning responsibilities and communication between objects — who talks to whom, when, and how loosely.
anchor: A theater rehearsal with fixed actors but a director endlessly redrawing WHO cues WHOM — the patterns are his laminated cueing diagrams.
example: Observer, Strategy, Command, State, Memento, Iterator, Visitor, Mediator...
confusables: Structural patterns — structural freeze object composition; behavioral choreograph runtime interaction and algorithm choice.
alternates: Ant colony signals — rejected, too diffuse to picture.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A subject keeps a list of subscribers and notifies them automatically when its state changes — one-to-many, publisher pushes.
anchor: A lighthouse blinks once and every ship's bell on the horizon rings itself — each ship had signed the lighthouse's ledger to be notified.
example: button.addEventListener('click', fn); RxJS subject.subscribe(observer)
confusables: Pub/sub — observers register directly WITH the subject; pub/sub inserts a broker so parties never know each other.
alternates: Newspaper delivery — reserved for pub/sub, which has the middleman.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface so the client can pick or swap them at runtime.
anchor: A caddie's golf bag: same golfer, same swing, but you pull driver, wedge, or putter per hole — the bag hands you an algorithm shaped like a club.
example: Collections.sort(list, comparator); compressor = new GzipStrategy()
confusables: State — strategy is chosen by the CLIENT and strategies ignore each other; states switch THEMSELVES as the object transitions.
alternates: Swiss army knife — rejected, one welded object, nothing injected.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Reifies a request as an object carrying receiver plus parameters, enabling queues, logs, retries, and undo.
anchor: A diner order spike: every shouted order becomes a paper ticket stabbed onto the spike — queueable, re-cookable, or torn up to undo.
example: editor.execute(new PasteCommand(clipboard)); Celery task queues
confusables: Strategy — command packages ONE invocation (verb plus args) to defer or undo; strategy packages an algorithm choice with no undo semantics.
alternates: Genie granting written wishes — rejected, undo is the load-bearing part.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: An object delegates behavior to a current-state object and swaps it on transitions, replacing sprawling conditionals.
anchor: A vending machine possessed by moods: the CoinInserted spirit grabs the wheel, then hands it to Dispensing. Same chassis, a new driver at every stage.
example: TCPConnection delegates open()/close() to Closed, Listening, Established objects
confusables: Strategy — identical UML, but states know their siblings and trigger their own transitions; strategies are independent and client-picked.
alternates: Werewolf phases — rejected, only two states and no delegation image.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Captures an object's private state in an opaque token so it can be restored later without breaking encapsulation.
anchor: A wax-sealed envelope of your diary page: the archivist stores it but can never read it; only YOU may crack the seal and become Tuesday-you again.
example: m = editor.save(); ...; editor.restore(m) — game save slots work this way
confusables: Command undo — command replays inverse operations; memento snapshots and reinstates whole state blobs.
alternates: Photograph of a room — rejected, photos are readable, mementos opaque.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A do-nothing implementation of an interface used in place of null, removing repetitive null checks from clients.
anchor: A cardboard-cutout security guard propped by the door: patrol() does nothing at all, but nobody ever trips over an empty guard post.
example: class NullLogger { log(msg) {} }; return Collections.emptyList() not null
confusables: Optional/Maybe — Optional forces callers to CHECK for presence; a null object silently absorbs calls with safe defaults.
alternates: Scarecrow — rejected, scarecrows actively scare, cutouts do nothing.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Executed commands are pushed onto a stack; undo pops and reverses them (or restores mementos), redo replays from a second stack.
anchor: Pancakes stack up as you type; Ctrl+Z peels the top pancake and un-fries it back into batter, while the redo plate waits to re-fry it.
example: undoStack.push(cmd); undo(): c = undoStack.pop(); c.unexecute(); redoStack.push(c)
confusables: Event sourcing — undo stacks are session-local UI history; event sourcing is the persisted system of record.
alternates: Rewinding a cassette — rejected, tape rewind is continuous, not discrete pops.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Observers that never unsubscribe stay strongly referenced by the subject, causing memory leaks and ghost notifications.
anchor: The lighthouse keeps ringing doorbells of houses whose owners moved out years ago — the copper wires (references) alone hold the empty houses up.
example: Fix: removeEventListener on teardown; or WeakReference listener lists
confusables: Generic memory leak — here the SUBJECT holds the reference, so 'unused' observers are uncollectable and still receive events.
alternates: Zombie mailing list — rejected, wires-holding-houses is more visual.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: In languages with first-class functions, a bare lambda replaces the one-method strategy class — same pattern, no ceremony.
anchor: The golf caddie is fired and replaced by a single floating glove: no bag, no clubs, you just hand over the bare hand — the function itself.
example: sorted(xs, key=lambda x: x.age) instead of writing an AgeComparator class
confusables: 'The pattern disappeared' — the intent (pluggable algorithm) remains; only the class boilerplate evaporated.
alternates: Naked chef without a restaurant — rejected as noise.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Provides sequential access to a collection's elements through a standard cursor interface without exposing internal structure.
anchor: A museum audio-guide wand: press NEXT and it leads you room by room in order — you never see the curator's storage maps or basement shelving.
example: for x in xs uses __iter__/__next__; Java it.hasNext()/it.next()
confusables: Iterable — the iterable is the collection that VENDS iterators; the iterator is the one-use cursor itself.
alternates: Pez dispenser — rejected, cute but destroys the collection as it goes.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A base-class method fixes an algorithm's skeleton and defers specific steps to subclass hook overrides.
anchor: A Mad Libs card: the plot is printed in permanent ink; subclasses may only scribble words into the blanks, then the card reads itself aloud.
example: JUnit setUp()/test/tearDown(); HttpServlet.service() dispatching to your doGet()
confusables: Strategy — template method varies steps via INHERITANCE, fixed at compile time; strategy swaps whole algorithms via composition at runtime.
alternates: Paint-by-numbers — rejected, blanks-in-a-story encodes hooks better.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Moves an operation out of a stable object structure into a visitor object; elements call accept(v) which calls back v.visitX(this).
anchor: A tax inspector walking a village: each house opens its OWN door (accept), and the inspector whips out exactly the right form for that house type.
example: ast.accept(prettyPrinter); compiler passes: TypeCheckVisitor, CodeGenVisitor
confusables: Iterator — iterator merely walks the elements; visitor dispatches type-specific operations via double dispatch.
alternates: Door-to-door salesman — rejected, sells one thing to all types.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Centralizes many-to-many communication: colleagues talk only to a mediator hub, which coordinates who reacts and how.
anchor: An air-traffic control tower: planes never radio each other directly — every 'may I land?' routes through the tower, or metal rains from the sky.
example: ChatRoom.send(msg, from) routes to members; dialog controller coordinating widgets
confusables: Observer — observer broadcasts one-to-many blindly; mediator encodes explicit pairwise coordination LOGIC inside the hub.
alternates: Switchboard operator — rejected, ATC adds the crash consequence.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Passes a request along a linked chain of handlers; each one either handles it or forwards it to the next.
anchor: An office complaint slip climbing desks: the intern shrugs and passes it up, the manager shrugs — the slip crawls upward until someone finally stamps it.
example: Express middleware fn(req, res, next); Java servlet filter chains
confusables: Decorator — same wrapping shape, but decorators ALL run to add behavior; chain handlers may short-circuit and one 'owns' the request.
alternates: Hot potato — rejected, potato holders never actually handle it.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Represents each grammar rule as a class and evaluates sentences by walking the resulting syntax tree.
anchor: A tiny UN inside your program: one translator booth per grammar rule; a sentence passes booth to booth down the parse tree until meaning drips out the bottom.
example: regex engines; SQL WHERE-clause evaluators; expr.interpret(context)
confusables: Visitor on an AST — interpreter puts eval() IN the node classes; visitor extracts operations out of them.
alternates: Rosetta stone — rejected, static artifact, no per-rule machinery.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Methods return the receiver (or builder) so calls chain into a readable sentence that executes at the end.
anchor: A sommelier sliding one glass down the bar through a chain of stations that each add a note - the same glass keeps traveling, collecting flavor, until someone finally drinks it (executes).
example: QueryBuilder().select('id').where('age > 21').limit(10).run()
confusables: vs builder pattern (603): builder is about assembling a complex product; fluent chaining is the SYNTAX builders often wear
alternates: domino line of method calls
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: 'Don't call us, we'll call you': frameworks and template skeletons invoke your code at the right moment; you never drive their control flow.
anchor: A casting agent snatches your headshot at the door: 'We'll call YOU.' Months later the phone rings with your one scene — the hook method.
example: React calls your render(); Spring calls your @Bean methods; you never call the framework's main loop
confusables: Dependency inversion principle — DIP concerns which ABSTRACTION you depend on; Hollywood concerns who holds control FLOW.
alternates: Butler who forbids entering the kitchen — rejected, casting call is the name.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: External iterators let the client pull items with next(); internal iterators take a callback and the collection drives the loop.
anchor: Museum two ways: grip the audio-wand and press NEXT yourself, or slump into the tram that drives past every exhibit while you just hand it your eyes (callback).
example: it.next() (external) vs xs.forEach(f) / xs.map(f) (internal)
confusables: Push vs pull streams — same duality: external is pull (client paces), internal is push (producer paces).
alternates: Buffet vs waiter service — rejected, tram ride is more distinctive.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Applying patterns speculatively adds indirection without need; reach for one only when its specific force is actually present.
anchor: A knight in five stacked suits of armor clanking off to fetch tea — AbstractTeaFactoryVisitorProxy — who can no longer bend his arm enough to pour.
example: One if/else beats a Strategy hierarchy for two stable cases
confusables: YAGNI — YAGNI rejects unneeded FEATURES; patternitis is unneeded STRUCTURE around features you do need.
alternates: Wrapping a single grape in six gift boxes — kept as backup image.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Organizes code into horizontal layers (UI, application, domain, data) where each layer depends only on those below it.
anchor: A wedding cake you may only eat top-down: each tier rests squarely on the tier beneath and never, ever licks upward.
example: Controller -> Service -> Repository -> Database
confusables: Hexagonal — layered stacks dependencies downward toward the DB; hexagonal points everything inward toward the domain.
alternates: Geological strata — rejected, no image of the no-upward-calls rule.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Puts the domain core at the center behind ports; adapters at the edges translate between the core and every external technology.
anchor: A queen bee in the center cell of a honeycomb: each of the six waxed walls has a socket, and worker bees plug tools in from outside — the queen never leaves.
example: Core defines OrderRepository port; PostgresOrderRepository adapter plugs in from outside
confusables: Layered — hexagonal is symmetric (DB and UI are both mere adapters); layered treats the database as the special bottom.
alternates: Castle with six gates — bees chosen to bind to domain 6's hexagon mnemonic.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A technology-neutral interface owned by the core that declares what the application needs or offers — the socket, not the plug.
anchor: USB sockets molded into the honeycomb's wax walls: the hive dictates each socket's shape, and any gadget arriving from outside must match the hole.
example: interface PaymentGateway { charge(amount) } — declared inside the domain module
confusables: Adapter — the port is the interface defined inside the core; the adapter is the implementation living outside it.
alternates: Ship's harbor — rejected, harbors receive anything, sockets enforce shape.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Driving (primary) adapters call INTO the core — HTTP controllers, CLIs; driven (secondary) adapters are called BY the core — DB, mail.
anchor: Left wall of the honeycomb: woodpeckers hammering requests IN. Right wall: the hive's own tubes squirting honey OUT into jars. Same walls, opposite arrows.
example: REST controller -> core (driving); core -> SmtpMailer (driven)
confusables: GoF Adapter — here 'adapter' means any tech-specific edge component, not interface conversion per se.
alternates: Mouth vs tail of a fish — rejected, arrows on one wall each are clearer.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Concentric rings — entities, use cases, interface adapters, frameworks — with all source dependencies pointing inward toward the domain.
anchor: An onion whose core never cries: knives, tears, and supermarket stickers stay on the outer skins; the center ring has never even smelled a fridge (framework).
example: UseCase imports Entity; Controller imports UseCase; never the reverse
confusables: Hexagonal — same spirit; clean/onion prescribe named rings, hexagonal just says core-plus-ports. All obey 'point inward'.
alternates: Tree rings — rejected, tree rings grow outward historically, wrong direction.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Source-code dependencies may only point inward: inner circles know nothing — not even names — of anything in outer circles.
anchor: A one-way pilgrimage road spiraling into a mountain shrine: carts roll inward only, and the monks inside have never once heard the market's name.
example: Domain never imports Spring, HTTP, or SQL; outer code implements domain-owned interfaces
confusables: Dependency inversion principle — DIP is the class-level technique; the dependency rule is the architecture-wide policy it enforces.
alternates: Whirlpool — rejected, whirlpools pull objects in, code must not flow.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A translating boundary that converts a legacy or external model into your own, so foreign concepts never leak into your domain.
anchor: A decontamination airlock between your gleaming lab and a rusty factory: every crate gets unpacked, scrubbed, and repacked into YOUR containers before entering.
example: LegacyCrmClient -> AclTranslator -> Customer (your model, your terms)
confusables: Plain adapter — an ACL translates whole MODELS and semantics between contexts, not just one interface's method signatures.
alternates: Customs checkpoint — rejected, customs inspects but does not repackage.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Keep entities and business rules in plain objects with zero framework imports, so the core outlives and ignores infrastructure churn.
anchor: A monk copying scripture with a feather quill while gadget salesmen pound on the monastery door — the manuscripts calmly outlive every gadget fad.
example: Domain layer: no @Entity, no HttpRequest — pure classes and functions only
confusables: 'No frameworks anywhere' — frameworks are fine in OUTER rings; the rule bans them only from the domain core.
alternates: Off-grid cabin — rejected, monk-vs-salesmen adds the churn outside.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Strict layering lets a layer call only the layer directly beneath it; relaxed layering permits skipping layers downward for pragmatism.
anchor: Two office towers: in one, the elevator only ever descends a single floor per ride (strict); in the other you may plunge straight from penthouse to basement archives.
example: Controller calling Repository directly = relaxed layering (skips Service)
confusables: Layer violation — skipping DOWNWARD can be sanctioned policy; any upward dependency is always a violation.
alternates: Ladder vs fire pole — kept as a backup pair.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Layers are logical separations within a codebase; tiers are physical deployment units — a 3-layer app can run on a single tier.
anchor: Wedding cake vs wedding venues: one cake's sponge tiers (layers) can all sit on a single table, or be couriered to three different cities (tiers).
example: Django app (3 layers) on one server = 1 tier; move DB to its own host = 2 tiers
confusables: N-tier marketing speak — count machines for tiers, count module boundaries for layers.
alternates: Org chart vs office buildings — rejected, cake ties back to 640.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A module hides its internals behind a small public interface; the boundary is where the contract lives and change stops propagating.
anchor: Castle walls with one guarded gate: merchants trade only at the gate's counter, and whatever chaos brews inside the walls never crosses the moat.
example: Java module exports; TypeScript index.ts re-exporting only the public API
confusables: Namespace/folder — a folder merely groups files; a boundary additionally enforces WHAT is visible and hides the rest.
alternates: Cell membrane — rejected, membranes leak by design.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Dependency counts quantify coupling: afferent Ca (who needs me), efferent Ce (whom I need), instability I = Ce/(Ca+Ce).
anchor: A trapeze artist wearing ropes: ropes others pull taut on her (Ca) hold her steady; ropes SHE grips outward (Ce) make her sway. Sway fraction = instability.
example: I near 0 = stable core lib; I near 1 = top-level app; JDepend/ArchUnit report these
confusables: Cohesion — coupling measures dependence BETWEEN modules; cohesion measures belonging-together WITHIN one.
alternates: Spiderweb strands — rejected, no in/out direction visible.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Group code by business capability, not technical layer: feature packages localize change; layer packages scatter every feature across the whole tree.
anchor: A hardware store reorganized by project instead of material: the build-a-birdhouse aisle holds its own nails, wood and paint, so one job touches one aisle.
example: orders/ (model+api+db together) vs models/, views/, controllers/ each holding a slice of orders
confusables: vs layered architecture (64x): layers can still exist INSIDE a feature package; the question is the top-level folder axis
alternates: bento box vs cafeteria line
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A framework that reads wiring configuration, builds the whole object graph, and injects dependencies automatically, managing lifetimes.
anchor: A robotic LEGO butler reads your blueprint at dawn and snaps the entire castle together before you wake — you never touch a single brick yourself.
example: Spring ApplicationContext; .NET IServiceCollection; Guice Injector
confusables: DI the pattern — DI needs no container; 'pure DI' wires by hand in main(). The container merely automates the wiring.
alternates: Automated warehouse robots — rejected, LEGO butler links to object graphs.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Dependencies arrive as constructor parameters, making them mandatory, visible, and enabling immutable, always-valid objects.
anchor: A spaceship that physically cannot launch until every crew member is strapped in at ignition — and the hatch welds itself shut after liftoff (immutability).
example: constructor(private repo: Repo) {} — compile error if a caller omits it
confusables: Setter/field injection — those allow half-initialized objects and hidden requirements; constructor injection fails fast at build time.
alternates: Bouncer at the object's birth — rejected as gross but memorable.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Mutual dependencies among packages weld them into one un-reusable, un-releasable lump; keep the dependency graph acyclic (ADP).
anchor: Three mountaineers roped in a closed circle: when one slips, all three dangle together — and no single climber can ever be rescued (released) alone.
example: A->B->C->A: touching C rebuilds all; fix by extracting an interface package
confusables: Class-level circular imports — same disease at file scale; ADP concerns released package/module units.
alternates: Ouroboros snakes — rejected, one snake hides that MULTIPLE parties are stuck.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A minimal core defines extension-point interfaces and discovers plugins at runtime, so features ship and load independently.
anchor: A pegboard power-tool wall: the bare drill body (core) accepts any snap-on head — sander, whisk, saw — sold years later by total strangers.
example: VS Code extensions; ESLint plugins; Java ServiceLoader discovery
confusables: Library use — the app calls a library; a plugin is called BY the core through the core's own interface (control inverted).
alternates: Game console cartridges — rejected, consoles run one cartridge at a time.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Components fetch dependencies from a global registry — an anti-pattern versus DI because it hides real dependencies and hurts testing.
anchor: Employees sneak to a dusty basement vending machine for their tools: the org chart (constructor) lists no tools at all — until tests find the machine empty and everything jams.
example: ServiceLocator.get('mailer') deep inside a method — invisible in any signature
confusables: DI container — the container injects from OUTSIDE at composition time; a locator is called from INSIDE, coupling code to the registry.
alternates: Junk drawer — rejected, vending machine encodes the global registry API.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: The single place near the entry point where the whole object graph is composed; nothing else news up long-lived collaborators.
anchor: One grand florist stand at the app's front door where every bouquet (object graph) is arranged before opening hour — no flowers are ever cut in back offices.
example: main() { app = new App(new PgRepo(cfg), new SmtpMailer(cfg)); app.run(); }
confusables: Scattered new()s — the smell it cures; construction knowledge lives in ONE root, not sprinkled through business code.
alternates: Mission control room — rejected, florist encodes assembling, not commanding.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Depend in the direction of stability: volatile packages may depend on stable ones, never the reverse.
anchor: Hammocks tied to old oaks, never to saplings: swinging sleepers (changing apps) hang off thick trunks (stable cores). Tie an oak to a sapling and both crash down.
example: app (I~0.9) -> utils (I~0.1) fine; core depending on an experimental lib = violation
confusables: Stable-abstractions principle — SAP adds that stable packages should also be ABSTRACT; SDP only orders the arrows.
alternates: Anchoring yachts to buoys — rejected, buoys are all equally unstable.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Splits UI into Model (state and logic), View (presentation), Controller (input handling); views render from the model.
anchor: A puppet theater: the puppet (view) dances on stage, the puppeteer's hands (controller) translate the audience's shouts, the script binder backstage (model) holds the story.
example: Rails: route -> UsersController -> User model -> ERB view
confusables: MVP — in MVC the view may read the model directly; in MVP a presenter mediates everything and the view stays passive.
alternates: Restaurant waiter/kitchen/menu — reserved: food metaphors used elsewhere.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A presenter takes all input, drives a passive view through an interface, and talks to the model — view and model never meet.
anchor: A ventriloquist (presenter) with a wooden dummy (view): the dummy holds no thoughts of its own, moving its jaw exactly as the hand inside commands.
example: Android pre-ViewModel: LoginPresenter calls LoginView.showError()
confusables: MVVM — MVP's presenter calls view methods explicitly; MVVM's viewmodel exposes state and lets data binding do the syncing.
alternates: Puppet on strings — rejected, already spent on MVC's stage.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A viewmodel exposes bindable state and commands; a data-binding layer keeps view and viewmodel in sync with no direct references.
anchor: A mirror-dance studio: the dancer (viewmodel) moves and the mirror (view) matches instantly — neither ever touches the other; the glass (binding) does all the work.
example: WPF, Knockout, Vue: <input v-model='name'> bound to a viewmodel field
confusables: MVP — MVVM replaces the presenter's explicit view calls with declarative bindings; the viewmodel never knows the view exists.
alternates: Shadow following you — rejected, shadows are one-way, binding is two-way.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Framework machinery auto-syncs view widgets and model fields in both directions, at the cost of harder-to-trace update flows.
anchor: Two buckets on a pulley rope through a window: pour water into either bucket and the rope instantly levels them — sometimes sloshing back and forth mysteriously at 3am.
example: Angular [(ngModel)]='user.name' — edits flow field<->input automatically
confusables: One-way binding — one-way re-renders the view FROM state only; edits return via explicit events, keeping the flow traceable.
alternates: Telepathic twins — rejected, buckets show the sloshing failure mode.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: UI built from self-contained components owning their markup, logic, and state, composed into trees like functions.
anchor: LEGO minifigs each carrying a tiny brain and wardrobe inside: snap a plaza together from figures, then snap one figure into a different set — it still works.
example: React: <App><Header><SearchBar/></Header></App>
confusables: Template partials — partials share markup only; components also encapsulate behavior and local state.
alternates: Modular sofa — rejected, sofa parts hold no behavior.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: State flows down as props and changes flow up as events or actions through one loop, making every mutation traceable.
anchor: A one-way water park: state pours down the slide into the views below; riders send wishes back up only via the message-balloon chimney (actions). No swimming upstream.
example: React: props down, onChange callbacks up; the Elm architecture loop
confusables: Two-way binding — the very thing it replaces; syncing both ways is convenient but obscures who changed what.
alternates: Salmon ladder — rejected, salmon famously DO swim upstream.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: All state lives in one store; views dispatch actions, pure reducers compute the next state, and views re-render from it.
anchor: A courtroom for every click: the action files a case (dispatch), the judge-reducer reads old law plus case and pens ONE new law book — the whole town re-reads it.
example: dispatch({type:'ADD_TODO', text}); reducer: (state, action) => newState
confusables: MVC — many controllers mutate models in place; Redux has one store and immutable transitions through pure functions.
alternates: 666 as the single all-seeing store — rejected, spooky but mechanism-free.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: When siblings must share state, move it to their closest common ancestor and pass it down, keeping one source of truth.
anchor: Two kids fight over one toy, so mom places it on the top shelf: now both must ask her (the common ancestor), and everyone sees the same toy.
example: React: temperature state moved from two inputs into the parent Calculator
confusables: Global store — lifting goes only as high as NEEDED; jumping straight to a global store couples everything to it.
alternates: Flag raised up a pole — rejected, no sibling conflict shown.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Container components fetch data and hold logic; presentational components just render props — data and looks kept separate.
anchor: A restaurant split in two: the kitchen (container) sources and cooks everything; the plating artist (presentational) only arranges whatever lands on the plate.
example: UserListContainer fetches, then renders <UserList users={users}/>
confusables: Custom hooks — hooks now often replace containers by extracting logic without an extra component layer.
alternates: Brain and face — rejected, kitchen/plating shows the data handoff.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Split hard-to-test boundary code into a thin humble shell and a testable core, pushing all logic out of the untestable part.
anchor: A shy stagehand whose only job is pulling the curtain rope: he makes zero decisions, so nobody ever needs to audition (test) him — the whole play lives elsewhere.
example: View just prints viewmodel fields; all formatting logic unit-tested in the viewmodel
confusables: Facade — a facade simplifies a subsystem for callers; a humble object exists to move logic OUT of an untestable edge.
alternates: Doorman with no keys — rejected, stagehand ties to UI's stage.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Components communicate by producing and reacting to events rather than calling each other, decoupling senders from receivers in time and knowledge.
anchor: A town-square bell: the baker rings 'bread's ready!' and walks away; whoever cares comes running. The baker knows no names and waits for no one.
example: OrderPlaced event -> email service, inventory, analytics each react independently
confusables: Request/response — a request needs the receiver up NOW and awaits an answer; an event is fire-and-forget to unknown listeners.
alternates: Nervous system — rejected, nerves are point-to-point wiring.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Producers publish to named topics on a broker; subscribers receive by topic — neither side ever knows the other exists.
anchor: Magazine subscriptions: writers mail issues to the 'Gardening' PO box; the postman fans copies out to the subscriber list. Authors never see a single address.
example: Kafka topic 'orders'; Redis PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE; Google Pub/Sub
confusables: Observer — observers register directly with the subject object; pub/sub interposes a broker and topic names between the parties.
alternates: Radio station — rejected, radio has no per-topic subscription list.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Thin events announce that something happened plus an ID; consumers call back to the source for details — small events, but coupled reads.
anchor: A doorbell rings with a note: 'package #42 arrived.' You still have to trudge to the depot and ask what's inside box 42.
example: {event:'OrderPlaced', orderId:42} -> consumer GETs /orders/42 for details
confusables: Event-carried state transfer — fat events carry the data along, so no callback query is ever needed.
alternates: Pager beeping a code — rejected, doorbell-plus-depot shows the callback.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Events carry the full relevant state so consumers keep local copies and never query the source — availability up, duplication and staleness accepted.
anchor: The drone drops the WHOLE parcel on your porch, not a claim ticket: your own pantry (local copy) fills up, and you never visit the depot again.
example: {event:'OrderPlaced', order:{id, items, total, address}} consumed into a local table
confusables: Event notification — notification sends a pointer (go ask); ECST sends the payload (never ask).
alternates: Newspaper with the full story — rejected, parcel pairs with 672's ticket.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Persist every state change as an immutable event; current state is derived by replaying the log, which is the system of record.
anchor: An accountant's ink ledger: nobody erases, ever; a mistake gets a correcting line, and today's balance is re-summed from page one whenever anyone asks.
example: Account balance = fold(Deposited, Withdrawn...); snapshots speed up replay
confusables: Audit log — an audit log is a side record; in event sourcing the log IS the primary data and state is just a projection.
alternates: Git commit history — good but overused; ledger is more visceral.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Splits the write model (commands, invariants) from read models (queries, projections) so each side scales and shapes data independently.
anchor: A restaurant with two doors: orders enter through the strict kitchen door (commands, checks), while diners browse the big glass buffet window (reads), pre-plated for speed.
example: POST -> domain aggregate; GET -> denormalized view table updated from events
confusables: Event sourcing — often paired but independent; CQRS is two models, ES is log-as-truth. You can do CQRS over a plain SQL DB.
alternates: Two-faced Janus — rejected, no read/write asymmetry in the image.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A long-running distributed transaction as a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action to undo on failure.
anchor: A trip booked in dominoes: flight, hotel, car click down in turn; when the car rental topples, gnomes sprint back up the line standing hotel and flight dominoes upright again (compensations).
example: ReserveFlight -> ReserveHotel fails -> run CancelFlight compensation
confusables: Two-phase commit — 2PC locks all parties for atomicity; sagas accept intermediate states and undo with business-level compensations.
alternates: Relay race passing a baton — rejected, no undo leg exists in relays.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Handlers detect and ignore duplicate deliveries — via message IDs or naturally idempotent writes — since brokers promise at-least-once.
anchor: A stamp collector gluing envelopes by serial number into an album: the same envelope delivered twice gets a shrug — 'already glued in' — and hits the bin.
example: if processed_ids.contains(msg.id): skip; or UPSERT instead of INSERT
confusables: Exactly-once delivery — a myth end-to-end; reality is at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing to simulate it.
alternates: Nightclub hand-stamp — rejected, stamps mark people, not messages.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Replicas may briefly disagree after a write; absent new updates all converge to the same state — reads can be stale meanwhile.
anchor: Village gossip: grandma hears the wedding news a full day after the baker does, but by Sunday mass every single villager tells the identical story.
example: DNS propagation; DynamoDB default reads; read-your-writes sessions as a remedy
confusables: Strong consistency — strong makes every read see the latest write, paying latency and availability (CAP) for the privilege.
alternates: Ripples settling in a pond — rejected, gossip shows per-replica lag.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Write events to an outbox table in the SAME DB transaction as the state change; a relay publishes them later — no lost or phantom events.
anchor: The love letter is sealed into the same envelope as the rent check: one lick, one stamp — both arrive or neither does. The mailroom clerk (relay) does the actual posting.
example: INSERT order; INSERT outbox(event); COMMIT; Debezium/poller ships rows to Kafka
confusables: Dual write — the bug it fixes: writing DB then broker separately can succeed on one and silently fail on the other.
alternates: Carbon-copy paper — rejected, envelope shows the atomic commit.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: One deployable with in-process calls versus many independently deployable services with network calls — simplicity traded for autonomy plus ops cost.
anchor: One granite boulder versus a mosaic of pebbles joined by strings: the boulder moves whole or not at all; pebbles travel alone, but the strings (network) fray and tangle.
example: One Rails app on one box vs Netflix's hundreds of services
confusables: Modular monolith — modules give boundaries WITHOUT the network; distribution is about deployment, not code structure.
alternates: Cruise ship vs flotilla — kept as a backup image.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Draw service lines around business capabilities that change together, so one team can deploy without synchronizing with others.
anchor: Cutting a birthday cake along the frosting roses, never through them: slice through a rose (capability) and both plates need each other's crumbs forever after.
example: Billing, Shipping, Catalog services — not 'the controllers service'
confusables: Bounded context — a great default source of boundaries; a service boundary adds deployment, team, and runtime autonomy on top.
alternates: Property fence lines — rejected, cake-rose encodes 'don't cut through'.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Publish breaking changes under a new explicit version while old versions keep serving, so clients migrate on their own schedule.
