anchor: A highway keeps the rusty old bridge open while the new one rises alongside: signs read '/v1 left lane, /v2 right' — and nobody's car falls into the river.
example: GET /v2/users; Stripe-Version header; media-type versioning in Accept
confusables: Backward-compatible change — additive changes (a new optional field) need NO new version; version only for breaks.
alternates: Software v1/v2 boxes on a shelf — rejected, bridges show parallel serving.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Evolve APIs additively — add optional fields, never rename, remove, or retype — while clients ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader).
anchor: Grandma's recipe card with extra sticky notes stapled on: old cooks simply ignore the staples and the cake still rises — but no one may ever cross out a line.
example: Protobuf: never reuse field numbers; JSON consumers skip unknown keys
confusables: Forward compatibility — backward: new server keeps old clients working; forward: old code tolerates NEW data it doesn't know.
alternates: Old key fitting a new lock — rejected, staples show additive-only.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Write and agree the API contract (OpenAPI, protobuf, AsyncAPI) before implementing; both sides generate code and test against it.
anchor: Architects sign blueprints before one brick is laid: plumber and electrician build in parallel to the same drawing, and the inspector (contract test) checks walls against paper.
example: openapi.yaml -> generate server stubs + client SDK; Pact contract tests in CI
confusables: Code-first with generated docs — docs derived from code drift with it; contract-first makes the spec the source of truth.
alternates: Prenup agreement — rejected, blueprints add the parallel-build payoff.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A dedicated backend per client type (web, mobile, TV) that aggregates and reshapes downstream APIs to that UI's exact needs.
anchor: Personal shoppers per customer: the mobile shopper packs a tiny pre-chewed lunchbox, the web shopper loads a full banquet cart — both raid the same warehouses.
example: Netflix: separate API edge services for iOS vs TV clients
confusables: API gateway — a gateway is one generic front door (auth, routing); a BFF is client-specific and owned by that client's team.
alternates: Custom-tailored suits — rejected, shoppers show the aggregation step.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Incrementally replace a legacy system by routing slices of traffic to new services growing around it, until the old core can be deleted.
anchor: A strangler fig vine wrapping a great old oak: root by root it steals the light, and years later the vine IS the tree — hollow bark where the oak once stood.
example: Proxy routes /invoices to the new service, everything else to legacy; migrate route by route
confusables: Big-bang rewrite — the fig migrates in shippable slices with rollback; a rewrite bets everything on one cut-over day.
alternates: Ship of Theseus — rejected, the fig is the pattern's actual name.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Services that must be deployed, versioned, or changed together — network overhead plus tight coupling; the worst of both worlds.
anchor: Chain-gang prisoners in separate cells: officially independent, yet shackled ankle-to-ankle straight through the walls — one man shifting drags every cell block.
example: Smells: shared database across services, lockstep releases, sync call chains 5 deep
confusables: Honest monolith — a monolith is coupling in-process, cheaply; the smell is PAYING distribution costs without gaining autonomy.
alternates: Synchronized swimmers in separate pools — kept as a comic backup.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A single entry point in front of services handling cross-cutting edge concerns — routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS — so each service doesn't.
anchor: A castle gatehouse: one drawbridge where guards check papers, count entrants, and point carts to the right courtyard — the inner keeps have no doors to the outside world.
example: Kong/Envoy/AWS API Gateway: /users -> user-svc after JWT check and rate limit
confusables: BFF — a gateway is one shared generic edge; a BFF is per-client and reshapes payloads for that specific UI.
alternates: Airport security funnel — rejected, gatehouse pairs with castle walls at 650.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: One deployable whose internal modules keep strict boundaries and own their data — microservice discipline without the network.
anchor: An apartment building with individually locked units and one street address: tenants (modules) cannot wander into each other's kitchens, yet there is exactly one front door to maintain.
example: Shopify's Rails core with packwerk-enforced component boundaries
confusables: Big ball of mud — the difference is ENFORCED module boundaries; mud has one deployable AND no interior walls.
alternates: Bento box — rejected, compartments suggest food not enforced locks.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: One precise shared vocabulary, spoken by developers and domain experts alike, used identically in conversation, models, and code.
anchor: A ship's crew who call every rope by its exact name: shout 'halyard!' and all hands grab the same line. Mutter 'that ropey thing' and the mast comes down.
example: Experts say 'the policy lapses' -> class Policy { lapse() } — never 'deactivate'
confusables: Company jargon — jargon drifts per department; ubiquitous language is deliberately unified WITHIN one bounded context.
alternates: Babel tower falling — rejected, encodes failure, not the discipline.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A domain object defined by a stable identity that persists through time, not by its attributes, which may all change.
anchor: A man with a barcode tattooed on his ankle: he ages, dyes his hair, changes his name twice — the scanner still beeps the same ID. He IS his barcode.
example: Customer #881 changes address and email — still the same Customer
confusables: Value object — swap every field of an entity and it is still 'it'; a value object with different fields IS a different value.
alternates: Passport holder — rejected, passports expire and get reissued.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: An immutable object defined entirely by its attribute values, with no identity; equal fields mean interchangeable objects.
anchor: Two identical 2x4 red LEGO bricks: shuffle them behind your back and nobody can ever tell. To 'change' one's color you don't repaint — you pick up a different brick.
example: Money(10,'EUR') == Money(10,'EUR'); LocalDate; Coordinates(lat, lng)
confusables: Entity — entities compare by ID and may mutate; value objects compare by all fields and should be immutable.
alternates: Two ten-euro notes — rejected: real banknotes carry serial numbers (identity).
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A cluster of entities and values with one root as sole entry point; the root enforces invariants and is saved as one transactional unit.
anchor: A grape bunch held only by its stem: to move, sell, or inspect any grape you must lift the stem (root). Pluck a grape directly and invariant juice spills everywhere.
example: Order (root) owns OrderLines; order.addLine() enforces the total; repo saves the Order whole
confusables: Plain object graph — an aggregate forbids outside references to its internals; only the root's ID crosses the boundary.
alternates: Keyring — rejected, keys hang independently with no invariants.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A collection-like abstraction for retrieving and persisting whole aggregates, keeping domain code free of query and storage detail.
anchor: A magic library counter: whisper 'Order 42' and the librarian slides you the whole bound volume; hand one back and it is filed. You never see the stacks (SQL).
example: orders.findById(id); orders.save(order) — interface in domain, impl in infrastructure
confusables: DAO — a DAO mirrors tables and rows; a repository speaks in whole aggregates and domain terms, one per aggregate root.
alternates: Coat-check booth — rejected, coats come back unchanged; aggregates evolve.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: An explicit boundary inside which one model and language hold consistently; the same word may map to a different model next door.
anchor: Two embassies on one street: inside each fence 'visa' means something precise — and different. Cross a gate and your papers must be re-translated.
example: 'Product' in Catalog (photos, copy) vs in Shipping (weight, dimensions)
confusables: Microservice — contexts are model and language boundaries; a service is a deployment unit. Often 1:1, but not necessarily.
alternates: Country dialects — rejected, dialects blur at borders; contexts are sharp.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Documenting relationships between bounded contexts — partnership, customer/supplier, conformist, ACL, shared kernel — and who adapts to whom.
anchor: A war-room map with strings between embassy pins, each string labeled 'who obeys whom': some pairs share a treaty (shared kernel), others hide behind translators (ACL).
example: Sales conforms to the legacy ERP's model; Payments shields itself via an ACL
confusables: Architecture diagram — boxes-and-arrows show calls; a context map shows POWER and model-translation relationships.
alternates: Family tree of in-laws — rejected, no direction of obedience.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: An immutable record, named in past tense in the ubiquitous language, of something meaningful that happened in the domain.
anchor: A town crier's scroll nailed to the market post: 'OrderShipped, this third of June!' — past tense, sealed in wax; anyone may read and react, no one may edit.
example: class OrderShipped { orderId, occurredAt }; published after the commit
confusables: Command — a command asks for something TO happen (imperative, refusable); an event states it already DID (immutable fact).
alternates: Birth certificate — rejected, certificates get amended; events never.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A stateless domain operation that spans multiple aggregates or fits no single entity, expressed in the ubiquitous language.
anchor: A freelance notary who owns no house: he walks between households (aggregates) to officiate exchanges no single family could sign alone, then leaves carrying nothing.
example: TransferService.transfer(fromAccount, toAccount, amount) — touches two aggregates
confusables: Application service — app services orchestrate use cases (transactions, auth, DTOs); domain services hold BUSINESS rules spanning entities.
alternates: Traveling referee — rejected, referees judge, notaries execute the deal.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: A smell where entities are bags of getters and setters and all behavior lives in service classes — OO shape without OO benefits.
anchor: A gym full of mannequins in workout clothes: perfectly shaped bodies (data) that cannot lift a single dumbbell; trainers (services) drag their limbs around for them.
example: OrderService.calcTotal(order) vs order.total() — logic exiled from its data
confusables: DTO — DTOs are SUPPOSED to be dumb carriers at boundaries; the smell is DOMAIN objects being that dumb.
alternates: Zombie models — rejected, zombies still move themselves; mannequins can't.
mnemonic: SIX sides of the hexagon - hexagonal architecture

definition: Data stored as relations: unordered tables of typed rows and named columns, addressed by value, never by position or pointer.
anchor: A strict cafeteria: every fact sits in a tray with fixed labeled compartments; trays stack into tables, and no compartment may hold two foods.
example: CREATE TABLE users (id INT, name TEXT, city TEXT); / Each row is one fact: (7, 'Ada', 'London') / Rows have no inherent order; queries filter by value
confusables: Spreadsheet — sheets address cells by position (B7); relations have no row order or cell coordinates, only values.
alternates: Excel-hall of steel tables (too generic office imagery).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Column(s) that uniquely and non-nullably identify each row; every table should have exactly one.
anchor: A hotel front desk: every room has exactly one brass key with a number stamped in; no two rooms share a number, and a blank key with no number is refused.
example: CREATE TABLE users ( / id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, / email TEXT);
confusables: UNIQUE constraint — UNIQUE allows NULLs and many per table; a PK is unique + NOT NULL and there is only one per table.
alternates: Fingerprint scanner at each row's door (less concrete than numbered hotel keys).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: A column holding another table's primary key value, linking child rows to their parent row.
anchor: A restaurant coat-check ticket #88 points to hook #88 in another room; the waiter (constraint) refuses to issue a ticket for a hook that doesn't exist — no orphan tickets.
example: CREATE TABLE orders ( / id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY, / user_id BIGINT REFERENCES users(id));
confusables: Primary key — the PK lives in the parent and is unique; the FK lives in the child, may repeat, and may be NULL.
alternates: Library call number pointing to a shelf (weaker orphan-prevention imagery).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Core query shape: FROM picks tables, WHERE filters rows, SELECT projects columns — logically evaluated in that order.
anchor: A fishmonger works right to left: nets the whole lake (FROM), throws back the small fish (WHERE), then fillets only the cuts you ordered (SELECT).
example: SELECT name, email / FROM users / WHERE created_at >= '2026-01-01';
confusables: Written order vs logical order — you type SELECT first, but the engine runs FROM, then WHERE, then SELECT.
alternates: Assembly line with three stations (not distinctive enough to recall).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: ORDER BY sorts the result set; LIMIT (with OFFSET) caps how many of the sorted rows come back.
anchor: A podium ceremony: all marathon finishers are lined up by time (ORDER BY), then only the first three climb the podium (LIMIT 3); everyone else goes home unlisted.
example: SELECT name, seconds FROM runners / ORDER BY seconds ASC / LIMIT 3;
confusables: GROUP BY — GROUP BY collapses rows into groups; ORDER BY only rearranges them, the row count is unchanged.
alternates: Nightclub queue with a rope after three people (podium encodes the sort step better).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Collapses rows sharing key values into one row per group, so aggregates (COUNT, SUM, AVG) summarize each group.
anchor: You sort a coin heap into labeled jars, then weigh whole jars. You may report a jar's label or its weight — never one particular coin; it melted into the group.
example: SELECT country, COUNT(*), AVG(age) / FROM users / GROUP BY country;
confusables: DISTINCT — DISTINCT only dedupes rows; GROUP BY builds groups you can run aggregates over.
alternates: Sorting-hat assigning houses (fun but carries no aggregate imagery).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Filters whole groups after aggregation, so its conditions can use aggregate results; WHERE cannot.
anchor: WHERE is the bouncer screening individual coins at the door; HAVING is a second bouncer who weighs the finished jars and tips out any jar under 100 grams.
example: SELECT country, COUNT(*) AS n / FROM users GROUP BY country / HAVING COUNT(*) > 100;
confusables: WHERE — WHERE screens individual rows before grouping; HAVING screens completed groups after aggregation.
alternates: Airport baggage scale rejecting heavy bags (loses the after-grouping timing).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: NULL means unknown: comparisons involving NULL yield UNKNOWN, so NULL = NULL is not true; test with IS NULL.
anchor: A masked stranger at the party: asked 'are you Bob?' they shrug (UNKNOWN). Even two masked strangers side by side cannot confirm they are the same person.
example: SELECT NULL = NULL; -- NULL, not true / SELECT * FROM users WHERE email IS NULL; / WHERE x <> 5 also drops rows where x IS NULL
confusables: Zero or empty string — those are known values; NULL is the absence of a value and poisons any comparison to UNKNOWN.
alternates: Schrödinger's cell holding both values (wrong: NULL is unknown, not superposed).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT combine two queries' rows vertically; UNION dedupes unless you say UNION ALL.
anchor: Two families hand in wedding guest lists. UNION merges them and crosses out the duplicate cousin; UNION ALL seats her twice; INTERSECT keeps only names on both lists; EXCEPT strikes everyone the other family invited.
example: SELECT city FROM stores / UNION / SELECT city FROM suppliers; -- UNION ALL keeps dupes
confusables: JOIN — joins glue columns side by side by matching keys; set ops stack rows from column-compatible queries.
alternates: Venn-diagram paint mixing (too abstract, no dedup story).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: SQL states what result you want; the optimizer chooses how — access paths, join order, and algorithms.
anchor: You tell the taxi driver 'the opera house', not turn-by-turn directions; the driver (query planner) knows tonight's traffic and picks the route. EXPLAIN is peeking over his shoulder.
example: You write: SELECT * FROM users WHERE age > 30 / Planner decides: index scan vs seq scan, / join algorithm, table order
confusables: Imperative code — loops spell out every step; declarative queries leave the steps to the planner.
alternates: Ordering a meal vs cooking it yourself (overused analogy, low distinctiveness).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Pairs rows from two tables where the join condition matches; rows with no partner appear nowhere in the result.
anchor: Speed dating night: only couples whose numbers match on both cards leave together into the results room; wallflowers without a match simply go home unrecorded.
example: SELECT o.id, u.name / FROM orders o / JOIN users u ON u.id = o.user_id;
confusables: LEFT JOIN — outer joins keep unmatched rows padded with NULLs; inner join silently drops them.
alternates: Zipper teeth meshing (doesn't show unmatched rows being dropped).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: LEFT, RIGHT and FULL joins keep unmatched rows from one or both sides, filling the missing columns with NULL.
anchor: A generous host: every guest from the left list gets a seat even without a date; the missing partners are cardboard cutouts labeled NULL. FULL OUTER seats both walls of wallflowers.
example: SELECT u.name, o.id / FROM users u LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id; / -- users with no orders show o.id = NULL
confusables: Inner join — inner returns only matched pairs; outer preserves the unmatched side(s) with NULL padding.
alternates: Noah's ark boarding singles too (muddles which side is preserved).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: A sorted side structure (usually a B-tree) mapping key values to row locations, turning full scans into O(log n) lookups.
anchor: The index at the back of a fat textbook: sorted terms with page numbers. You jump 'polymorphism -> p.412' instead of reading 900 pages; the book itself stays unsorted.
example: CREATE INDEX idx_users_email ON users(email); / SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='a@b.c' / -- descends 3-4 index pages, then fetches the row
confusables: Primary key — a logical uniqueness rule (usually backed by an index); an index is the physical lookup structure itself.
alternates: Library card catalog drawers (dated; a textbook's back index is more universal).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: An index on (a, b) serves filters on a, or on a and b — but not on b alone; column order decides usefulness.
anchor: A phone book sorts by last name, then first. Finding 'Smith' or 'Smith, John' is instant; finding every 'John' regardless of surname means reading the entire book.
example: CREATE INDEX ON people (last_name, first_name); / WHERE last_name='Smith' AND first_name='John' -- uses it / WHERE first_name='John' -- cannot
confusables: Two single-column indexes — separate indexes can't act as one sorted (a,b) structure; order within one index is what matters.
alternates: Dictionary sorted by second letter (negative example, harder to recall).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: An index containing every column a query needs, so the engine answers from the index alone — an index-only scan, no table fetch.
anchor: The index card already has the whole answer written on its back — the librarian answers from the card drawer without ever walking to the filing cabinet.
example: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, status, total); / SELECT status, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7; / -- index-only scan: heap never touched
confusables: Composite index — composite is about multiple key columns; covering means the query needs nothing beyond the index.
alternates: All-inclusive resort wristband (vague link to 'no extra fetch').
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: The fraction of rows a predicate keeps; indexes shine when few rows match and lose to full scans when most rows do.
anchor: Searching 'female patients' in a maternity ward — the index shrugs, nearly every row matches. Searching one passport number is a needle the index hands you instantly.
example: WHERE passport_no='X99' -- 1 of 10M rows: index wins / WHERE active=true -- 80% of rows: / planner picks a seq scan; the index would thrash
confusables: Cardinality — cardinality counts distinct values in a column; selectivity is the fraction of rows a specific filter passes.
alternates: Panning for gold vs scooping sand (loses the 'index useless when common' half).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Shows the optimizer's chosen plan — scans, join order and algorithms, row estimates; the ANALYZE variant executes and adds real numbers.
anchor: X-ray glasses for your query: put them on and its skeleton appears — a fat Seq Scan femur right where you swore an index lived.
example: EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=7; / Seq Scan on orders (cost=0.00..4582 rows=98750) / -- no index used; estimates vs actuals visible
confusables: EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE — plain EXPLAIN only estimates; ANALYZE really runs the query and reports true times and row counts.
alternates: Fortune teller predicting the query's path (planner is deterministic, not mystical).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Every INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE must also maintain each index on the table, so each extra index slows every write.
anchor: An author with twelve secretaries: each sentence he writes, all twelve re-file cards in their own catalogs. A thirteenth catalog makes lookups snappier and his pen heavier.
example: Table with 6 indexes: / one INSERT = 1 heap write + 6 index updates / Bulk-load trick: drop indexes, load, rebuild
confusables: 'Indexes always help' — they help the reads that use them; every write pays for all of them whether used or not.
alternates: Toll booths on the write highway (doesn't scale visually with index count).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Code fetches a list with one query, then loops issuing one query per item — N+1 round trips instead of one join or batched query.
anchor: A waiter takes a 30-guest table's order, then makes thirty separate sprints to the bar, one drink per trip, instead of one loaded tray. The kitchen is fine; the hallway is the bottleneck.
example: users = q('SELECT * FROM users') # 1 / for u in users: / q('SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id=%s', u.id) # +N
confusables: Slow query from a missing index — each N+1 query may be fast; the killer is round-trip count, fixed by eager loading or IN-batching, not an index.
alternates: Woodpecker pecking one hole per seed (less tied to request/response trips).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Engines match rows via nested loop (small or indexed inner), hash join (big unsorted inputs), or merge join (both inputs sorted).
anchor: Pairing socks three ways: hold each sock against every other (nested loop); toss them into color bins and match within bins (hash); or sort both piles and zip down them in step (merge).
example: Nested loop: outer 10 rows, inner has index / Hash: build hash of small table, probe with big / Merge: both sorted on key, single zip pass
confusables: Join types (INNER/LEFT) — types define which rows belong in the result; algorithms only define how the engine finds them.
alternates: Speed dating vs name-tag tables (speed dating already anchors inner join).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Structuring tables so every fact is stored exactly once, removing redundancy by decomposing along functional dependencies.
anchor: Marie Kondo for data: every fact gets exactly one drawer; a duplicated fact sparks no joy and is folded away into its own table, leaving a key behind as the receipt.
example: Instead of orders repeating user_name, user_addr: / users(id, name, addr) + orders(id, user_id) / Address change: 1 row, not 400
confusables: Denormalization — the deliberate reverse: reintroducing duplication for read speed once you know the cost.
alternates: Prime factorization of tables (mathy, not sensory).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Redundancy breeds update anomalies (miss one copy), insert anomalies (fact needs a host row), and delete anomalies (fact dies with its row).
anchor: The teacher's address is copied onto all 30 student cards. She moves and one card is missed (update); a teacher with no students can't be stored anywhere (insert); the last student leaves and her address is shredded with the card (delete).
example: employees(name, dept, dept_phone): / phone changes -> update 40 rows, miss 1 -> two truths / delete last employee -> dept phone vanishes
confusables: Concurrency anomalies (dirty/phantom reads) — those come from parallel transactions; these come from redundant schema design.
alternates: Hydra heads regrowing wrong info (monster imagery too vague on mechanism).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Every column holds one atomic value per row — no arrays, comma lists, or repeating groups; multi-values become extra rows.
anchor: One egg per carton cup. Someone crammed three phone numbers into one cup; the lid won't close until each egg gets its own cup — or its own carton row.
example: Bad: phones = '555-1, 555-2, 555-3' / Good: user_phones(user_id, phone) / one row per number
confusables: 2NF — 1NF is about atomic cells; 2NF is about columns depending on the whole composite key.
alternates: No Russian-doll cells (dolls suggest nesting depth, not comma lists).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: 1NF plus no partial dependency: every non-key column must depend on the whole composite key, not just part of it.
anchor: A safe that needs both keys (order_id + product_id) to open — yet 'product price' pops out with the product key alone. It never belonged in this safe; escort it to the products vault. The WHOLE key.
example: order_items(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name) / product_name depends on product_id alone -> partial / move it: products(product_id, product_name)
confusables: 3NF — 2NF removes dependencies on part of the key; 3NF removes non-key columns depending on other non-key columns.
alternates: Half a ticket stub gets you in (weak: half stubs sometimes do get you in).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: 2NF plus no transitive dependency: non-key columns may not depend on other non-key columns — nothing but the key.
anchor: A gossip chain: the row tells zip, zip tells city — city learned the key's secret secondhand. Cut out the middleman: zip and city elope to their own table. Nothing but the key, so help me Codd.
example: people(id, zip, city): zip -> city is transitive / split: people(id, zip) + zips(zip, city) / city stored once per zip
confusables: BCNF — BCNF additionally forbids non-candidate-key determinants even when the dependent column is part of a key.
alternates: Train car pulled by the wrong engine (mechanism unclear at recall time).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Stricter 3NF: every determinant (left side of any functional dependency) must be a candidate key — no exceptions.
anchor: Bouncer-Codd at the club door: anyone caught determining anything ('this tutor fixes the course') must flash a full candidate-key membership card. Mere column cliques are thrown out and given their own venue.
example: (student, course) -> tutor, but tutor -> course / tutor determines yet isn't a candidate key / decompose: tutors(tutor, course) + enroll(student, tutor)
confusables: 3NF — 3NF tolerates a non-key determinant when the dependent is part of some key; BCNF tolerates nothing.
alternates: Acid-test pun on Boyce (collides with ACID at 731).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Deliberately duplicating or precomputing data to cut joins and speed reads, accepting extra write logic and drift risk.
anchor: The barista tapes the top ten recipes to the espresso machine instead of walking to the recipe book. Pours are instant — but when HQ changes the mocha, she must remember every taped copy or serve the old drink.
example: orders.items_count kept by trigger / vs COUNT(*) join on every page load / faster read, one more thing to keep true
confusables: Unnormalized design — denormalized is a measured step back from a normalized model; unnormalized never had one.
alternates: Cheat sheet tucked in the exam sleeve (moral flavor distracts from trade-off).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Analytics layout: a central fact table of measured events joined to small denormalized dimension tables — who, what, when, where.
anchor: A sheriff's star: the fat metal center is the fact table (every sale stamped with numbers), and each point of the star is a dimension — who bought, what item, which store, what day.
example: fact_sales(date_id, store_id, product_id, qty, rev) / dim_date, dim_store, dim_product / query: join facts to a few dims, aggregate
confusables: Snowflake schema — snowflake re-normalizes dimensions into sub-tables; star keeps each dimension flat and wide.
alternates: Solar system with planet lookups (orbits suggest motion, not joins).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Surrogate keys are meaningless generated IDs; natural keys are real-world attributes whose meaning can change, collide, or leak.
anchor: The prison files inmates by number, not name: names get remarried, misspelled, and duplicated; number 24601 never changes no matter what Jean Valjean calls himself this year.
example: id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY -- surrogate / vs PRIMARY KEY (email) -- natural / email changes -> every referencing FK must change
confusables: UUID vs auto-increment — both are surrogates; that choice is about generation and index locality, not business meaning.
alternates: SSN as the key (SSN is itself a cautionary natural key — confusing as an anchor).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Storing data as generic entity-attribute-value rows for 'flexibility', losing types, constraints, and sane queries in the bargain.
anchor: A furniture store that sells every chair as a bin of loose screws with sticky notes: 'color: red', 'legs: 4'. Infinitely flexible shelving — but rebuilding one chair takes forty trips, and nothing stops 'legs: banana'.
example: attrs(entity_id, attr, value) / (42,'color','red'), (42,'legs','4') -- all TEXT / one product = N self-joins; no CHECK possible
confusables: JSONB column — a typed, indexable document kept in one row; EAV shreds each attribute into its own untyped row.
alternates: Junk drawer of Post-its (junk drawer is reserved for schema-on-read).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: A group of statements executed as one all-or-nothing unit: COMMIT makes all of it visible; ROLLBACK erases every trace.
anchor: A magician's tablecloth yank: either the whole new table setting appears in one motion, or the trick fails and every plate is exactly where it was. The audience never sees half-moved cutlery.
example: BEGIN; / UPDATE acc SET bal=bal-100 WHERE id=1; / UPDATE acc SET bal=bal+100 WHERE id=2; COMMIT;
confusables: Single autocommit statement — each statement is already its own tiny transaction; BEGIN binds several into one fate.
alternates: Airlock with both doors (airlocks encode sequencing, not atomicity).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules still hold), Isolation (concurrent txns don't interfere), Durability (committed survives crashes).
anchor: Drop a committed transaction into a vat of acid: it stays in one piece (A), keeps its lawful shape (C), doesn't react with its vat-mates (I), and the etching it leaves is permanent (D).
example: Crash between debit and credit -> both roll back (A) / CHECK bal >= 0 still true after (C) / power cut after COMMIT -> transfer survives (D)
confusables: BASE — BASE systems trade per-transaction guarantees for availability, converging eventually instead of immediately.
alternates: Invisible-ink lemon juice (fading ink contradicts durability).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Reading another transaction's uncommitted changes; if it rolls back, you acted on data that never officially existed.
anchor: Reading a friend's essay over their shoulder mid-edit and quoting a sentence they delete a second later — your citation points at words that never made the published page.
example: T1: UPDATE acc SET bal=0 (not committed) / T2: SELECT bal -> 0, ships a refund / T1: ROLLBACK -- T2 refunded money that never moved
confusables: Non-repeatable read — that one re-reads committed changes; a dirty read sees changes that were never committed at all.
alternates: Reading tomorrow's newspaper before printing (weaker cause-and-effect).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Within one transaction, re-reading the same row returns a different value because another transaction committed an update in between.
anchor: You check the hotel room price, walk off to fetch your wallet, and return to the same screen in the same session — the same room now costs more. Same row, same query, two answers.
example: T1: SELECT price WHERE id=7 -> 100 / T2: UPDATE price=120; COMMIT / T1: SELECT price WHERE id=7 -> 120 (same txn)
confusables: Phantom read — phantom is new rows appearing in a re-run range query; non-repeatable is one existing row changing value.
alternates: Heraclitus' river, never the same row twice (too philosophical to discriminate).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Re-running a range query inside one transaction returns new rows that another transaction inserted and committed meanwhile.
anchor: You count twelve ghosts in the ballroom, blink, count again: thirteen. None of the originals changed — a phantom matching your WHERE clause materialized between counts.
example: T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE age>60 -> 12 / T2: INSERT senior; COMMIT / T1: same COUNT -> 13; a new row appeared
confusables: Non-repeatable read — that is an existing row changing; phantom is the membership of the result set changing.
alternates: Whack-a-mole rows (moles also disappear — phantoms only appear).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: A ladder trading anomalies for concurrency: read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, serializable — each rung blocks more anomalies.
anchor: Hotel privacy tiers: glass walls (neighbors see your dirty drafts), curtains (you see only finished rooms), a locked door (your view frozen at check-in), and a private floor where stays replay as if guests came one at a time.
example: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; / Postgres default: READ COMMITTED / serializable may abort: catch and retry
confusables: Consistency (the C in ACID) — that is about domain rules holding; isolation is about what concurrent transactions can see.
alternates: Volume knob on interference (a knob lacks the four named stops).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Proceed without locks; at write time verify a version or timestamp hasn't changed — if it has, abort and retry. Best when conflicts are rare.
anchor: Two wiki editors type freely on the same page. On save, the site compares version numbers: first saver wins; the second sees 'page changed since you loaded it — reapply'. Nobody waited; one redid work.
example: UPDATE docs SET body=:new, version=version+1 / WHERE id=7 AND version=:seen; / -- 0 rows updated => conflict: reload and retry
confusables: Pessimistic locking — pessimism blocks rivals up front; optimism never blocks and detects conflicts at commit time.
alternates: Handshake deal checked by a notary later (notary timing too vague).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Acquire the lock before touching the data so no rival can modify (or lock) it until you finish; everyone else queues.
anchor: The office bathroom-key school of concurrency: take the key off the hook before you go; everyone else shuffles in the hallway, even those who only wanted to check the mirror.
example: BEGIN; / SELECT * FROM inventory WHERE sku='A1' FOR UPDATE; / -- rival writers block here until COMMIT
confusables: Optimistic locking — optimism lets everyone work and rejects late writers; pessimism makes late arrivals wait at the door.
alternates: Calling dibs on the last slice (dibs isn't enforced — locks are).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: A row-locking read inside a transaction: locks the selected rows so your read-then-write sequence can't be interleaved by rivals.
anchor: You lay your flat hand on the bakery's last éclair while fishing out your wallet. Everyone may still look at it, but nobody can grab or reprice it until you finish paying (COMMIT).
example: BEGIN; / SELECT bal FROM acc WHERE id=1 FOR UPDATE; / UPDATE acc SET bal=bal-100 WHERE id=1; COMMIT;
confusables: Plain SELECT in a transaction — ordinary reads take no row locks; FOR UPDATE holds the rows until commit.
alternates: Reserved parking cone (cones get moved; row locks don't).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, waiting forever; the database detects the cycle and aborts one as the victim.
anchor: Two overpolite people wedged in a doorway, each holding the door the other needs, bowing 'after you' forever — until the manager (the engine) shoves one back outside (abort) so the other passes; the ejected one retries.
example: T1: locks row A, wants B / T2: locks row B, wants A / ERROR: deadlock detected -- fix: lock rows in same order
confusables: Ordinary lock wait — blocking ends when the holder commits; a deadlock is a cycle only a victim abort can break. | cf. 530 Deadlock (déjà pris): same wait cycle, but the database detects it and kills one victim transaction automatically
alternates: Gridlocked intersection (the stock OS-course image; the doorway bow is fresher).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Non-relational stores that give up joins, strict schemas, or full ACID to win scale, flexibility, or speed for specific access patterns.
anchor: Across from the strict relational cafeteria, a food-truck park: each truck serves one dish its own way — no shared menu, no table service, no substitutions, and the lines fly.
example: Redis (key-value), MongoDB (document), / Cassandra (wide-column), Neo4j (graph) / pick per workload, not by fashion
confusables: NewSQL — NewSQL keeps SQL and ACID while scaling out; NoSQL changes the data model itself.
alternates: Wild-west data saloon (lawlessness overstates it; each store has strict rules).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Stores an opaque value under a unique key; you can GET, SET, and DELETE by exact key but never query inside the value.
anchor: A wall of gym lockers: present exactly key #417 and get your bag. Ask the attendant 'which lockers contain red jackets?' and he just stares — lockers are opaque; only keys open anything.
example: SET session:abc '{user:7}' EX 3600 / GET session:abc -> '{user:7}' / -- no WHERE, no query by value
confusables: Document store — documents are queryable and indexable by inner fields; a KV value is a sealed blob.
alternates: Valet claim ticket (coat-check already anchors foreign keys).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Stores JSON-like documents with nested structure, indexed and queried by inner fields; the document is the unit of atomicity.
anchor: Each customer is one manila folder: orders stapled inside, addresses paper-clipped to the flap. You pull the whole folder in one motion — no reassembling a person from ten separate drawers.
example: db.users.find({'address.city': 'Oslo'}) / db.users.updateOne({_id:7}, {$push:{orders:o}}) / -- one document updated atomically
confusables: Key-value store — KV can't see inside its values; a document DB indexes and filters on nested fields.
alternates: Russian nesting dolls (nesting yes, but retrieval-as-one-unit is lost).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Rows keyed by a partition key hold sparse dynamic columns sorted by a clustering key; built for huge, write-heavy, partitioned workloads.
anchor: A mile-wide spreadsheet where each row grows its own private set of labeled columns; the wall is sawn into panels by row key and the panels are shipped to different warehouses (partitions).
example: Cassandra: PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), ts) / partition by user, rows time-sorted inside / great: feeds, sensor series; bad: ad-hoc joins
confusables: Columnar format (Parquet) — despite the name, wide-column stores are row-oriented per partition; columnar is a scan-optimized file layout.
alternates: Hotel corridor of doors per guest (spatial metaphor tangles rows and columns).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Nodes and edges are first-class records with direct pointers, so multi-hop relationship traversals stay fast regardless of dataset size.
anchor: A detective's corkboard: photos (nodes) joined by red string (edges). 'Friend of a friend of a friend' is walking three strings with your finger — no re-sorting file cabinets (joins) at every hop.
example: MATCH (a:Person {name:'Ada'})-[:FRIEND*2..2]->(f) / RETURN f.name / -- friends-of-friends in one traversal
confusables: Join table in SQL — models the same edges, but each hop costs a join; graph engines follow stored pointers per hop.
alternates: Subway map of relationships (maps are static; traversal is the whole point).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent: replicas may briefly disagree but converge; availability beats instant consistency.
anchor: The alkaline answer to ACID: a spilled BASE spreads slowly across the lab counter until it evenly coats it (replicas converge eventually) — and the counter stays usable the whole time (available).
example: cart on two replicas briefly differs / partition heals -> versions reconcile / user never saw an error page
confusables: ACID — ACID promises every transaction sees consistent data now; BASE promises the system converges later.
alternates: Gossiping villagers eventually all know (gossip is a protocol, saved for the distributed domain).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Data is written without enforced structure; each reader applies a schema at query time, so interpretation is deferred and may vary.
anchor: A junk drawer you fill freely for years; sorting happens only at the moment a hand goes in. Each family member imposes a different order — batteries by size, or by 'probably dead'.
example: raw JSON logs land in S3, no table upfront / df = spark.read.schema(s).json('s3://logs/') / two teams read the same files differently
confusables: Schemaless — data always has implicit structure; schema-on-read merely moves enforcement from write time to read time.
alternates: Rorschach inkblot data (implies there is no true structure at all).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: In NoSQL, model tables and keys from the exact queries you must serve — not from entity shape — because ad-hoc joins don't exist.
anchor: The chef stocks each station for tonight's menu, not alphabetically: the garnish sits beside the plate it lands on. Orders (queries) fly out because the layout mirrors them; an off-menu request means re-prepping the kitchen.
example: DynamoDB: list the queries first: / 'orders by user by date' -> PK=user_id, SK=order_date / a new query pattern may need a new GSI/table
confusables: Entity-relationship modeling — relational designs entities first and trusts joins for any query; NoSQL bakes the query into the layout.
alternates: Tailored suit vs off-the-rack (fit metaphor carries no query imagery).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Document modeling choice: nest related data inside the parent (one fast read, duplication) or store an ID to fetch separately (one copy, extra trip).
anchor: Scrapbooking: glue the photo onto the page (embed — instant to view, but a shared photo is re-printed onto every page) or write 'see album B, photo 12' (reference — one original, an extra walk to the shelf).
example: Embed: {order:1, items:[{sku,qty}...]} one read / Reference: {order:1, item_ids:[9,12]} / + second query; items deduped across orders
confusables: SQL foreign key — a document reference is app-resolved with no enforced integrity; an FK is engine-enforced and joinable.
alternates: Backpack vs locker for books (lockers already anchor key-value stores).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Using several database types in one system, each chosen for the workload it serves best, at the cost of operating them all.
anchor: One hospital, many archives: X-ray films in the imaging vault, blood samples in the cold fridge, appointments in the front ledger. One patient, three purpose-built stores — and three systems for the night shift to keep alive.
example: Postgres: orders and money / Redis: sessions; Elasticsearch: product search / S3: images -- one app, four stores
confusables: Multi-model database — one engine exposing several models; polyglot runs separate specialized engines side by side.
alternates: Swiss Army knife (backwards — polyglot is many tools, not one gadget).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: A small fast store holding copies of hot data so repeat reads skip the slow source; effectiveness lives and dies by hit ratio.
anchor: The fridge is downstairs, so your desk's top drawer holds the snacks you actually keep reaching for. The drawer is tiny — every new snack squeezed in shoves a neglected one out.
example: v = redis.get(k) # ~0.1 ms / if v is None: v = db.query(k) # ~5 ms / 99% hit ratio -> DB sees 1% of reads
confusables: Memoization / CPU cache — same principle at other layers; this tier caches data between app and database (e.g. Redis).
alternates: Squirrel's nut stash (hoarding misses the 'copy of a slower source' point).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: The app checks the cache first, on miss reads the database itself, then writes the result back into the cache; the cache stays passive.
anchor: You open the snack drawer yourself; it's empty, so YOU trudge to the fridge and, walking back, drop a copy in the drawer for next time. The drawer never restocks itself — it's a dumb box.
example: v = cache.get(k) / if v is None: / v = db.get(k); cache.set(k, v, ttl=300)
confusables: Read-through — there the cache itself fetches from the source on a miss; in cache-aside the application does the fetching.
alternates: Sticky note left for future you (notes don't expire or evict).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: The app only ever asks the cache; on a miss the cache itself loads the value from the backing store, returns it, and keeps it.
anchor: A vending machine with a tiny stocker living inside: you only ever press the button. If the slot is empty, his arm reaches back into the warehouse, loads the slot, and the can drops — you never see the warehouse.
example: cache = Caffeine.newBuilder() / .build(key -> db.load(key)); / v = cache.get(k) // miss handled inside
confusables: Cache-aside — the app does the DB round trip there; read-through hides the source behind the cache API.
alternates: Butler fetching from the cellar (butlers also take writes — muddles the pattern).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Writes go to the cache and synchronously to the backing store before acknowledging; never stale, but writes pay full latency.
anchor: A carbon-copy pad: one pen stroke writes the top sheet (cache) and presses through to the ledger page beneath (database) in the same motion. The stroke drags a little — but the sheets can never disagree.
example: def put(k, v): / db.write(k, v) # sync / cache.set(k, v) # ack only after both
confusables: Write-behind — behind acknowledges first and flushes later (fast, can lose data); through is synchronous and safe.
alternates: Twin scribes writing simultaneously (two agents suggest race conditions).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Writes hit the cache and are acknowledged immediately, then flushed to the backing store asynchronously — fast, but a crash loses unflushed writes.
anchor: The bartender chalks your rounds on a slate instantly and settles with the register in one batch at closing. Lightning service — but if a spilled beer wipes the slate before settling, those rounds never happened.
example: cache.set(k, v); ack() # instant / queue.push((k, v)) / # flusher writes queue to DB every 5s
confusables: Write-through — through waits for the store before acking; behind acks first and gambles on the flush.
alternates: Postbox emptied nightly (mail loss feels rare; a wiped slate is visceral).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Each entry carries a time-to-live; past it the entry counts as gone, bounding staleness without any invalidation logic.
anchor: Every cache entry parks at its own meter. When the meter hits zero the tow truck hauls the data away, however shiny the car — freshness by countdown, no judgment involved.
example: SET price:sku42 '9.99' EX 60 / -- worst case: 60s stale / no purge code needed when the price changes
confusables: LRU eviction — eviction reacts to capacity pressure; TTL removes by age even in a half-empty cache.
alternates: Milk expiry stamp (use-by dates say 'maybe fine'; parking meters are absolute).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Purging or updating every cached copy exactly when the source changes is notoriously error-prone — one of the two hard things in CS.
anchor: You change your phone number, then must hunt down every place the old one lives: friends' phones, forms, the fridge magnet, grandma's book. Miss one and someone confidently dials the wrong number for years — a stale cache.
example: UPDATE products SET name='X2' WHERE id=42; / copies: Redis, CDN, materialized view, browser / purge all, in order, race-free -- or serve lies
confusables: TTL expiry — TTL is the blunt workaround that accepts bounded staleness; invalidation is the precise, hard, event-driven purge.
alternates: Recalling gossip from a village (gossip imagery belongs to distributed protocols).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: When full, the cache evicts by recency (LRU: least recently used) or by frequency (LFU: least frequently used) to make room.
anchor: A stuffed closet: LRU tosses whatever you wore longest ago; LFU counts wears and tosses the least-worn. The tux worn once last night survives LRU's purge but is first out under LFU.
example: @functools.lru_cache(maxsize=1000) / Redis: maxmemory-policy allkeys-lru / (or allkeys-lfu for frequency)
confusables: TTL — TTL removes entries because they are old; eviction removes them because the cache is full.
alternates: Musical chairs for data (that's random eviction — wrong policy).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: When a hot key expires, many concurrent misses hammer the source at once; fix with per-key locks, TTL jitter, or serving stale while one refreshes.
anchor: The bakery's 'fresh until 9:00' sign flips and the whole queue charges the tiny kitchen at once. Smart baker: one runner fetches the new tray (lock) while everyone else gets yesterday's croissant (stale), and tomorrow's sign flips at 9:07 (jitter).
example: if cache.miss(k): / if lock.acquire(k): v = db.get(k); cache.set(k,v) / else: v = cache.get_stale(k) # or brief wait
confusables: Ordinary cache miss — a stampede is thousands of simultaneous misses on one hot key, not a single cold read.
alternates: Black Friday doors opening (crowd yes, but no expiry trigger in the image).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Cache the fact that a lookup found nothing, so repeated misses for the same absent key stop hitting the store; keep its TTL short.
anchor: The doorman keeps a pencil list of names NOT on the guest list. The same gatecrasher returns five times: five glances at the not-list, zero trips to the ledger inside. He erases it often — people do get invited eventually.
example: u = cache.get('user:999') / if u == 'NOT_FOUND': return 404 # no DB hit / cache.set('user:999','NOT_FOUND', ttl=30)
confusables: Regular caching — this stores absence, not values; too long a TTL makes newly created items look missing.
alternates: Bouncer's banned-photo wall (bans are permanent; negative entries must expire).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Converting in-memory structures into a byte or text sequence for storage or transfer, and deserializing them back on the other side.
anchor: IKEA logic: the assembled chair (object graph, pointers as glued joints) can't ship. Flatten it into a labeled box of parts (bytes) with instructions; the buyer rebuilds an identical chair in a different living room (process).
example: data = json.dumps({'id': 7, 'tags': ['a']}) / send over network / write to disk / obj = json.loads(data) # other process or language
confusables: Serializable isolation level — unrelated despite the name: that is transaction ordering, not encoding objects to bytes.
alternates: Freeze-drying astronaut food (rehydration loses the pointer-flattening nuance).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Ubiquitous text format of objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null — human-readable and schema-free; no comments, dates, or safe ints past 2^53.
anchor: Jason, the friendly courier every country understands: travels light, speaks plainly, checks no ID (schema). But he can't pronounce dates — he hands them over scribbled as strings — and drops any coin bigger than 2^53.
example: {"id": 7, "tags": ["a", "b"], / "ts": "2026-07-10T12:00:00Z"} / -- the date is just a string by convention
confusables: JavaScript object literal — JSON is stricter: double-quoted keys, no comments, no trailing commas, no functions.
alternates: Argonauts' cargo manifest (myth pun too oblique for fast recall).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Indentation-structured, human-first format beloved for config; comments and anchors, but whitespace is syntax and unquoted scalars get coerced.
anchor: A poem whose meaning hangs on indentation — nudge one space and a stanza changes parents. In the last line the country code NO freezes into boolean false: Norway, voted out of existence by YAML 1.1.
example: server: / port: 8080 / country: NO # YAML 1.1 reads false; quote 'NO'
confusables: JSON — YAML adds comments, anchors, multi-line strings; but JSON never turns NO into false or breaks on a stray space.
alternates: Jenga tower of spaces (instability yes, coercion traps lost).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Tag-based markup with attributes, namespaces and XSD validation — verbose, strict about well-formedness, still core to enterprise and documents.
anchor: Data in full Victorian dress: every value is announced on arrival AND departure — <name>Ada</name> — chaperoned by namespaces and corseted by a schema. Ceremonious and heavy, but nobody sneaks in unvalidated.
example: <order id="7"> / <item sku="A1" qty="2"/> / </order> validated against an XSD
confusables: HTML — HTML is forgiving display markup for browsers; XML is strict data markup that dies on one unclosed tag.
alternates: Bureaucratic forms in triplicate (forms imagery reserved for constraints).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Binary format with a compiled .proto schema; fields travel as numbers, not names — tiny, fast, typed, with codegen per language.
anchor: A military telegram in dense number code: 'field 1: 7, field 3: Ada' — no names on the wire, just numbered slots. Both ends drill from the same codebook (.proto); lose the codebook and the bytes are gibberish.
example: message User { / int64 id = 1; / string name = 2; } // wire: tag numbers + values
confusables: Avro — Avro ships or registers the schema with the data; protobuf assumes both sides already compiled the codebook.
alternates: Morse code operators (Morse encodes characters, not typed numbered fields).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Binary row format whose schema travels with the data (file header or registry ID), enabling clean schema resolution between versions.
anchor: A shipping container with the packing manifest riveted to its door: any dock, even one that has never seen this shipper, unloads it by reading the attached schema; old docks reconcile new manifests line by line (schema resolution).
example: Kafka + Schema Registry: / record bytes start with schema id 42 / reader fetches schema 42, resolves vs its own
confusables: Protobuf — protobuf's schema is compiled into both ends and absent from the wire; Avro's schema accompanies the data.
alternates: Passport stapled to luggage (passports identify people — weaker fit).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Columnar file format: each column's values stored contiguously with compression and statistics, so scans read only the columns they need.
anchor: A parquet floor laid in long strips — each board strip is one column running the whole room. Refinishing the 'price' strip never touches the other boards, and identical boards in a strip compress into one stamped plank.
example: df.write.parquet('s3://sales/') / SELECT AVG(amount) FROM sales / -- reads only 'amount' column chunks + stats
confusables: Avro — Avro is row-oriented, ideal for streaming whole records; Parquet is columnar, ideal for scanning few columns of many rows.
alternates: Sliced loaf vs whole sandwiches (food again; the floor pun encodes the name).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Changing a serialized schema while old and new programs interoperate: backward = new reader reads old data; forward = old reader reads new data.
anchor: Cassette decks across generations: your new deck still plays grandma's old tapes (backward); her old deck plays your new mixtape by skipping tracks it doesn't recognize (forward). House rule: add tracks with defaults, never reuse a track number.
example: safe: add optional field with a default / unsafe: rename, retype, or reuse field id 3 / registry enforces BACKWARD / FORWARD / FULL
confusables: Database schema migration — that mutates live tables with DDL; evolution keeps readers and writers of encoded records compatible.
alternates: Chameleon changing skins (no reader/writer pairing in the image).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Byte order for multi-byte numbers: big-endian stores the most significant byte first, little-endian the least; mismatches scramble binary data.
anchor: Gulliver's Lilliputians wage war over which end of the egg to crack first. Your 4-byte integer sails between their shores: 0x01020304 lands as 04 03 02 01 on the little-endian beach — same egg, opposite crack.
example: 0x01020304 -> bytes: / big-endian: 01 02 03 04 (network order) / little-endian: 04 03 02 01 (x86, most ARM)
confusables: Character encoding (UTF-8) — encoding maps characters to bytes; endianness orders the bytes within one numeric value.
alternates: Reading direction of scripts (invites confusion with text encodings).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Serialize instants as ISO 8601 UTC (or epoch), never ambiguous local formats; never put money in binary floats — use integer cents or decimals.
anchor: Two grenades hide in every payload: a clock and a coin. The clock stamped 01/02/03 explodes into three different days on three continents; the coin dropped into float acid dissolves to 0.30000000000000004. Defuse with ISO 8601 UTC and integer cents.
confusables: Storing local wall-clock time — right for future human events (meetings follow local rules); past instants belong in UTC.
alternates: Y2K flashback (Y2K was digit width, not zone/precision ambiguity).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: The fixed-size block (commonly 8KB) that engines read, write, cache, and lock; rows live inside pages and all I/O moves whole pages.
anchor: This library never lends a sentence — you must check out the whole 8KB pamphlet even to read one line. Every cart, shelf, and reading desk (buffer pool) moves pamphlets, never loose sentences (rows).
example: Postgres default page: 8KB / reading one 40-byte row still does 8KB of I/O / pages are the buffer-pool and WAL-image unit too
confusables: OS memory page (4KB) — same idea one layer down; the engine's page is its own on-disk and buffer-pool unit.
alternates: Egg-crate shipping (the egg carton already anchors 1NF).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Keeps rows in a balanced, very wide tree of sorted pages; point reads and updates edit pages in place — read-optimized, the mature default.
anchor: A banyan tree pruned absurdly wide and shallow: trunk to any of a billion leaves in three or four hops. Repairs are carved directly into the leaf where the fruit hangs (in-place update), keeping the whole tree forever sorted.
example: MySQL InnoDB, Postgres B-tree indexes / height ~3-4 levels for billions of keys / point read = one root-to-leaf descent
confusables: Binary search tree — one key per node and towering height; B-tree nodes pack hundreds of keys so the tree stays squat and disk-friendly.
alternates: Corporate org chart with wide spans (org charts aren't sorted structures).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Buffers writes in a memtable, flushes sorted immutable files, merges them in background — random writes become sequential appends; write-optimized.
anchor: A chef's order spike: new tickets stab on instantly (memtable — fast writes). A full spike is frozen and filed as a sorted stack (SSTable flush); finding an old order means rummaging several stacks until the night porter merges them (compaction).
example: RocksDB, Cassandra, LevelDB / write: append WAL + memtable insert (fast) / read: memtable, then newest-to-oldest SSTables
confusables: B-tree engine — B-trees update pages in place, favoring reads; LSM appends and merges, favoring write throughput at read cost.
alternates: Sedimentary rock layers (nice layers, but the in-memory buffer stage is missing).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Every change is appended and fsynced to a sequential log before data pages are touched; replaying the log after a crash restores committed work.
anchor: The captain's iron rule: write the maneuver in the logbook before touching the sails. When the storm (crash) hits mid-turn, the surviving mate replays the logbook line by line and the ship ends exactly where the entries promised.
example: COMMIT = WAL record fsynced (sequential, fast) / data pages updated lazily later / crash -> replay WAL from last checkpoint
confusables: Audit trail — the WAL is physical, engine-internal, recycled after checkpoints; an audit trail is business-level and kept for humans.
alternates: Dear-diary-before-the-heist trope (the nautical replay is crisper).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Immutable files of sorted key-value pairs flushed from the memtable; served via sparse indexes and bloom filters, never edited — only superseded.
anchor: Each flush freezes a mini-dictionary in perfect alphabetical order. Nobody writes in a frozen book — corrections appear in a newer volume that shadows the old entry, and a doorman (bloom filter) swears which volumes definitely lack your word.
example: flush memtable -> users-000123.sst (sorted, frozen) / bloom filter: 'definitely absent' for cheap / sparse index -> one seek into the file
confusables: Memtable — the mutable in-RAM stage; SSTables are its frozen, sorted, on-disk descendants.
alternates: Amber-fossilized data (amber preserves one insect, not sorted runs).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Background merge of overlapping SSTables into fewer files, keeping newest versions and dropping tombstoned deletes — pays I/O now for faster reads later.
anchor: A Zamboni for the dictionary stacks: between periods it glides over ten scratched-up frozen volumes, merges them into one smooth sheet, and scrapes the dead entries (tombstones) off as ice shavings.
example: 10 SSTables, key x appears 3 times -> / compact to 1 file: newest x kept, tombstones gone / fewer files = fewer seeks per read
confusables: VACUUM (Postgres) — vacuum reclaims dead MVCC row versions in mutable heaps; compaction merges immutable LSM files.
alternates: Spring-cleaning garage sale (selling isn't merging; the Zamboni encodes 'one smooth sheet').
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Keeps multiple versions of each row; every transaction reads a consistent snapshot, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
anchor: A museum that hands each visitor time-stamped photocopies: you tour the collection exactly as it looked when you entered, while artists repaint originals in the same halls. Nobody waits; a janitor (VACUUM) later shreds copies no visitor can still see.
example: Postgres: UPDATE writes a new row version (xmin/xmax) / older snapshots still see the prior version / VACUUM reclaims versions no txn can see
confusables: Lock-based concurrency — locking makes readers and writers queue; MVCC gives readers snapshots so they never queue behind writers.
alternates: Git branch per reader (git is a whole VCS; overloads the metaphor).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: The engine's RAM cache of hot pages: reads hit memory instead of disk, and dirty pages are flushed back at checkpoints; hit ratio rules performance.
anchor: The librarian keeps the most-asked-for pamphlets heaped on her front desk; regulars never see the stacks. Pencil edits made on desk copies (dirty pages) are walked back to the shelves on periodic rounds (checkpoints).
example: Postgres shared_buffers, InnoDB buffer pool / 99% hit ratio: most reads never touch disk / dirty pages flushed at checkpoint
confusables: Query result cache — that stores final answers to whole queries; the buffer pool caches raw pages that every query shares.
alternates: Bedside book pile (no write-back story in a bedside pile).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Contiguous access vastly outruns scattered seeks — brutal on HDDs, still real on SSDs — so engines turn random writes into sequential logs and appends.
anchor: A record needle gliding along one groove pours out music (sequential); the DJ lifting and dropping the arm across tracks (random) buys a silent second per jump. The WAL and LSM exist to keep the needle in the groove.
example: HDD: ~150 MB/s sequential vs ~100 IOPS random / SSD: gap narrows but sequential still wins / (prefetch, erase blocks, queue depth)
confusables: Throughput vs latency in general — this is specifically about access pattern: the same device is orders faster when access is ordered.
alternates: Supermarket aisle sweep vs scavenger hunt (shopping imagery already overused).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Forces the OS to flush its buffered writes for a file down to durable media before returning; without it, written data can vanish on power loss.
anchor: 'It is written' means nothing until the wax seal: fsync presses the ring into hot wax and waits for it to harden. Skip it and your letter was merely spoken to the mail clerk (OS page cache), who may not survive the night.
example: f.write(data) # app buffer / f.flush() # to OS cache / os.fsync(f.fileno()) # to disk -- durable
confusables: flush() — flush moves data from app buffers into the OS cache; only fsync forces the OS cache onto durable media.
alternates: Notarized signature (notaries certify content, not persistence).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: OLTP: many tiny concurrent reads/writes touching single rows (row stores). OLAP: few huge scans aggregating millions of rows (column stores).
anchor: Downstairs, checkout lanes beep thousands of tiny basket updates a minute (OLTP). Upstairs at midnight, one accountant reads EVERY receipt of the year to ask how bananas did (OLAP). Different rooms, different filing.
example: OLTP: UPDATE cart SET qty=2 WHERE id=9; / OLAP: SELECT region, SUM(rev) FROM sales_5y / GROUP BY region;
confusables: HTAP — hybrid engines try both in one system; the classic split is row store for OLTP, columnar warehouse for OLAP.
alternates: Heartbeat vs annual physical (medical mapping strains quickly).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Extract from sources, transform (clean, conform, join) in a processing layer, then load the polished result into the warehouse.
anchor: Airport customs before entry: luggage is pulled off the plane (extract), opened, inspected and repacked in the customs hall (transform), and only cleared bags roll into the country — the warehouse (load). Nothing dirty crosses the border.
example: nightly: pull Postgres + CSVs (E) / Spark cleans, dedupes, conforms (T) / load dim/fact tables into warehouse (L)
confusables: ELT — the letters swap: ELT loads raw data first and transforms inside the warehouse with SQL.
alternates: Car wash before the garage (a wash tunnel is too passive to encode transform).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Load raw data straight into the warehouse, then transform it there with SQL (dbt et al.); cheap storage and elastic compute made raw-first practical.
anchor: Moving day: the truck dumps every box straight into the garage (load raw). You unpack inside at leisure with the house's own tools (SQL transforms) — and next year you can re-unpack differently, because the original boxes are still there.
example: Fivetran/Airbyte copy raw tables to Snowflake / dbt models: staging -> marts, all in SQL / re-run anytime; the raw layer is untouched
confusables: ETL — ETL transforms before loading, so raw data never lands; ELT keeps raw data queryable and re-transformable.
alternates: 'Eat now, digest later' pun (bodily humor fades fast under review).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Process accumulated data in scheduled bounded chunks; high throughput and simple retries, at the cost of latency until the next run.
anchor: The hamper fills all week; Sunday's one big wash handles everything at once — cheap per sock, and a ruined load just gets washed again (rerun). But Tuesday's mustard stain sits there until Sunday (latency).
example: 02:00 cron: spark-submit daily_job.py / processes yesterday's partition ds=2026-07-09 / failure? rerun the whole day idempotently
confusables: Stream processing — streams handle each event on arrival (seconds); batch waits for the scheduled window (hours).
alternates: Monthly payday (money metaphor better saved for exactly-once).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Continuously process unbounded event flows as they arrive, using windows, state, and watermarks for late data; low latency, higher complexity.
anchor: A sushi conveyor: each plate is handled the instant it glides past — nothing piles up. The chef groups plates into five-minute windows and holds each window open a grace period for plates stuck behind a slow customer (watermark).
example: Kafka -> Flink job scores each txn in <1s / window: 5 min tumbling, watermark 30s late / state lives inside the stream processor
confusables: Message queue — a queue only delivers events; stream processing computes over the flow with windows, joins, and state.
alternates: River fishing with hourly nets (nets are just batches in disguise).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Central analytics store of cleaned, modeled, schema-enforced tables (facts and dimensions), columnar underneath, built for fast SQL aggregation.
anchor: A museum, not a storage unit: every exhibit was cleaned, verified and labeled before display (schema-on-write); visitors (analysts) wander the curated halls asking anything. Nothing enters uncatalogued.
example: Snowflake / BigQuery / Redshift / analysts: SELECT ... FROM fact_sales JOIN dim_* / fed by ETL/ELT pipelines
confusables: Data lake — the lake stores raw files of any shape; the warehouse stores curated, typed, query-ready tables.
alternates: Costco of clean data (bulk shopping implies raw goods, wrong direction).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Cheap object storage holding raw files in any format, schema applied on read; flexible and vast — ungoverned, it degrades into a data swamp.
anchor: A reservoir: raw water pours in from every stream untested — logs, CSVs, images. Anyone may dip a bucket, but each drinker filters at the shore (schema-on-read). Fire the park rangers (catalog, governance) and it silts into a swamp.
example: s3://lake/raw/events/2026/07/10/*.json.gz / Athena/Spark apply schema at query time / catalog (Glue/Unity) or nobody finds anything
confusables: Lakehouse — adds table formats with ACID and schema (Iceberg, Delta) atop lake files, blending warehouse behavior into the lake.
alternates: Attic of unopened boxes (garage boxes already anchor ELT).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Analytics reads touch only the queried columns, and same-typed neighboring values compress hard — often ~100x less I/O than row storage.
anchor: Ask a full stadium the average age: the column store passes down one thin ribbon listing only ages — similar numbers that zip together tightly. The row store instead hands you every fan's entire wallet, ticket stubs and all.
example: 1B rows x 50 cols, query touches 1 col: / columnar reads ~2% of bytes, then compresses / row store drags all 50 columns per row
confusables: Wide-column store (Cassandra) — a row-oriented OLTP design despite the name; columnar is a physical layout for scan speed.
alternates: X-raying just the spine (the X-ray already anchors EXPLAIN).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Split a table or dataset into parts by a key (usually date) so queries prune to relevant partitions and old data can be dropped wholesale.
anchor: An ice-cube tray for events: each day freezes into its own cube. Asking about Tuesday pops out one cube — nobody thaws the whole freezer (full scan). Retention is snapping off a stale cube, not chiseling the block.
example: CREATE TABLE events (...) PARTITION BY RANGE (ds); / WHERE ds='2026-07-09' -- scans 1 of 365 / DROP PARTITION for retention: instant
confusables: Sharding — sharding spreads data across machines for write scale; partitioning splits within one dataset for pruning and lifecycle.
alternates: Filing cabinet by month (cabinets are everywhere in this domain; cubes pop).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Design jobs so reruns produce the same final state — overwrite the target partition, dedupe by key — making retries and backfills safe.
anchor: A rubber stamp, not a tally pen: stamping the same page five times leaves one clean mark. The intern with the tally pen re-counts on every rerun, and Monday's revenue doubles each time the job hiccups.
example: INSERT OVERWRITE TABLE sales PARTITION (ds='2026-07-09') / run twice -> same rows, no double counting / (vs INSERT INTO: each rerun duplicates)
confusables: Exactly-once delivery — a transport guarantee; idempotence makes at-least-once delivery safe by construction, the practical path.
alternates: Elevator button pressed repeatedly (hackneyed; the stamp shows state overwrite).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Database-enforced rules catch bad data from every path — app bugs, cron jobs, manual SQL; app validation is UX, the constraint is the guarantee.
anchor: App validators are polite greeters at the front door, easily bypassed via the side entrance (admin script, 2 a.m. psql). The constraint is the vault's steel door in the only corridor — every path funnels through it, and it never sleeps.
example: Rails validates :email, presence: true # skippable / update_all, raw SQL, other services bypass it / DB UNIQUE/NOT NULL/FK/CHECK cannot be bypassed
confusables: Application validation — friendlier errors, but only on paths that run it; a constraint binds every writer of the table.
alternates: Goalkeeper as last line (sports cliché; says nothing about multiple attack paths).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Declares that a column can never hold NULL, so every row must supply (or default) a value; the cheapest data-quality win there is.
anchor: A paper form with a mousetrap under one box: leave it blank and SNAP — the whole form (row) is rejected at the counter. No half-filled forms ever enter the archive.
example: email TEXT NOT NULL / INSERT INTO users(name) VALUES ('Ada'); / ERROR: null value violates not-null constraint
confusables: DEFAULT — a default fills in a missing value at insert; NOT NULL also rejects an explicit NULL.
alternates: Seatbelt chime that never stops (chimes nag; constraints refuse).
mnemonic: SEVEN normal forms to tame your tables

definition: Guarantees no two rows share the same value(s) in the constrained column(s), enforced by a unique index; NULLs typically don't count as duplicates.
